<!-- Source: configuration/profiles-and-prompts.md -->

# Profiles & Prompts

A profile defines the tool set, default permission stance, prompt guidance, and manifest defaults a session starts with. The system prompt is assembled from named markdown sections that can be overridden per profile, in settings, or via CLI flags.

## Built-in profiles

Select a profile with `--profile`, the top-level `profile` setting, or `session/create.profile` over the wire protocol. The default is `code`.

| Profile | Tools | Unmatched side-effecting calls | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `base` | none | policy default | Minimal contract; useful for pure chat or as a base for custom profiles. |
| `code` | `bash`, `read`, `grep`, `history`, `edit`, `write`, `fetch`, `codemode` | `allow` | Default profile. Ships coding-agent guidance in its `profile` section. |
| `search` | `read`, `grep` | `allow` | Read-only exploration profile. |

Additional tools are attached automatically when applicable:

- `jobs` and `cancel_job` are added by the core whenever a profile links a tool that supports background execution (such as `bash`).
- `finish` is added when `finish.schema_file` is configured.

## Disabling tools globally

Use `tools.disabled` to strip tools from every profile a settings file runs under:

```yaml
tools:
  disabled: [codemode, fetch]
```

- Naming a tool the active profile does not offer is ignored.
- Naming a tool the binary does not link, or a core-managed tool (`jobs`, `cancel_job`, `finish`), is an error.
- Disabling every tool a selected profile offers is an error, and such a profile is omitted from the binary's profile list.

## Named profiles

Define custom profiles under `profiles` in your settings file, then select them by name anywhere a profile is accepted:

```yaml
profiles:
  reviewer:
    base: code
    prompt_file: prompts/reviewer.md
    prompt_append: Focus on correctness and regressions.
    model_family: true
    feeds: [apron-room]
    feeds_defaults: false
    cli_registry_defaults: false
    mcp_defaults: false
    mcp_servers: [github]
    tools:
      disabled: [edit, write, bash, codemode]
```

### Profile fields

| Field | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `base` | string | Required. Names a built-in linked profile or another defined profile. |
| `prompt_file` | string | Absolute path, `~/...`, or path relative to the settings file (or profiles file). Read when opening a new session, not when listing profiles. Replaces the `profile` prompt section without replacing `base` or tool sections. |
| `prompt_append` | string | Inline text appended to the `profile` section after the base's prose (or after `prompt_file` if both are set). Mutually exclusive with `prompt_append_file`. |
| `prompt_append_file` | string | File form of `prompt_append`, resolved against the same directory as `prompt_file`. Mutually exclusive with `prompt_append`. |
| `model_family` | bool | Off unless set to `true`. Enables the `family` prompt section keyed by the chat model's `prompt_variant` (ships `gpt-5.6`, `gpt-6`, and `gpt-6.2`). An unknown or unset variant leaves the prompt unchanged. |
| `feeds` | list of strings | Feed manifest names this profile declares it needs; adds to the base's feeds (deduplicated). This is a presence assertion, not a filter: `feeds.paths` still controls which feeds load, and every loaded feed runs. A declared feed that is not loaded is skipped with a warning rather than failing the session. |
| `feeds_defaults` | bool | Overrides `feeds.defaults` for sessions under this profile. Omitting it keeps the top-level setting. |
| `cli_registry_defaults` | bool | Overrides `cli_registry.defaults` for sessions under this profile. Omitting it keeps the top-level setting. |
| `mcp_defaults` | bool | Overrides `mcp.defaults` for sessions under this profile. Omitting it keeps the top-level setting. |
| `mcp_servers` | list of strings | [MCP servers](/capabilities/mcp-servers) this profile's sessions start, by server name; adds to the base's selection (deduplicated, first-appearance order). `mcp.paths` still controls which manifests load; a selected server that is not loaded is skipped with a warning, and no server starts without a selection. |
| `tools.disabled` | list of strings | Tool exclusions added on top of global `tools.disabled`. Exclusions do not alter [permission rules](/operations/permissions-and-safety) or sandbox the remaining tools. |

An explicit `system_prompt.replace`, or a `system_prompt` rule that sets or removes the `profile` section, takes precedence over `prompt_file`, `prompt_append`, and `prompt_append_file`. A resumed session keeps the prompt recorded in its log once it has run.

## Layering with `profiles_files`

To keep large profile definitions out of your main settings file, move them into separate files listed under `profiles_files`:

```yaml
profiles_files:
  - profiles.yaml
  - team/profiles.yaml
```

Each file uses the same vocabulary under a top-level `profiles` key:

```yaml
profiles:
  slim:
    base: code
    feeds_defaults: false
    cli_registry_defaults: false
    mcp_defaults: false
```

- **Format:** Determined by file extension — YAML (`.yaml` / `.yml`) or JSON (`.json`).
- **Strict validation:** Unknown keys, unreadable files, or a file declaring zero profiles fail the load.
- **Precedence:** The settings file's own `profiles` map wins over `profiles_files`. Within `profiles_files`, the first file that defines a profile name wins over later files.
- **Path resolution:** Relative entries in `profiles_files` resolve against the settings file's directory. Relative `prompt_file` and `prompt_append_file` paths inside a profiles file resolve against that profiles file's own directory, so a profiles file travels with its prompts.

## REPL default profile (`repl_profile`)

`repl_profile` sets the profile used by the [interactive REPL](/getting-started/repl) when invoked without `--profile`:

```yaml
profile: code
repl_profile: reviewer
```

- Scoped to the REPL only: `poo run` and `poo serve` continue to use `--profile` or the top-level `profile` setting.
- Applies only when the REPL starts a new conversation; a reopened session runs under the profile recorded in its session log.
- Must name a profile known to the binary.

## System prompt sections (`system_prompt`)

The system prompt is composed from named sections rendered in this order:

1. `persona` — single-line identity header
2. `base` — core operating contract
3. `profile` — active profile's instructions
4. `family` — model-family guidance (when `model_family: true`)
5. `tools` — per-tool sections (`tools.<name>`) in tool offer order
6. `catalog` — [CLI registry](/capabilities/cli-registry) catalog (when applicable)
7. `skills` — [skills](/capabilities/skills) catalog
8. `environment` — working directory, OS, and session date (`YYYY-MM-DD`)
9. `user` — operator instructions (`session.user_prompt` / `session.user_prompt_file`)
10. `project` — project instructions (`session.project_prompt`)
11. Custom sections added via `system_prompt.sections` (in insertion order)

Configure overrides under `system_prompt`:

```yaml
system_prompt:
  base_file: prompts/base.md
  append: Always cite file paths with line numbers.
  sections:
    style: Keep answers under five sentences.
  remove:
    - environment
```

| Field | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `base_file` | Replaces the `base` section with the file's contents. Relative paths resolve against the settings file; `~/` resolves under the home directory. Mutually exclusive with `replace`. CLI override: `--system-prompt`. |
| `replace` | Replaces the entire prompt with literal text, dropping the default sections. Mutually exclusive with `base_file`. |
| `append` | Appends text to the `base` section. CLI override: `--append-system-prompt` (prefix with `@` to read from a file). |
| `sections` | Map of `name: text` entries that replace an existing section or append a new custom section. |
| `remove` | List of section names to drop. Removing a section that is not present is a no-op. |

For embedding-level prompt customization with Go `fs.FS`, see [Custom Tools & Prompts](/extending/custom-tools-and-prompts).

## Project and user instructions

### `session.project_prompt`

Enable per-project instructions with `session.project_prompt: true` (or `--project-prompt`):

```yaml
session:
  project_prompt: true
```

- Reads `AGENTS.md`, or `CLAUDE.md` if `AGENTS.md` is absent, from the session's working directory only — it never walks up to parent directories.
- Populates the `project` section and is read per session from that session's working directory.
- Capped at 64 KiB (`65536` bytes); longer files are truncated at a UTF-8 rune boundary with a truncation notice.
- A directory with neither file adds no section; an unreadable or non-regular file is an error.

### `session.user_prompt` and `session.user_prompt_file`

Add operator-level instructions that apply across projects to the `user` section:

```yaml
session:
  user_prompt: true
  # Or point to an explicit file (enables user instructions on its own):
  # user_prompt_file: ~/.config/poo/my-instructions.md
```

- Read once when building the runtime, not per session.
- `session.user_prompt: true` reads `AGENTS.md` from poo's platform config directory. If that default file does not exist, it is silently skipped.
- `session.user_prompt_file` (or `--user-prompt-file`) names an explicit file (supports `~/`) and enables user instructions without setting `session.user_prompt: true`. Because an explicit path is a promise, a missing file fails the build.
- Precedence: `--user-prompt-file` > `session.user_prompt_file` > `session.user_prompt`.

## Inspecting the rendered prompt

Run `poo prompt` to print the exact rendered system prompt a session would send to the model:

```bash
poo prompt --profile code --project-prompt
```

Pass `--pretty` for human-readable output with `--- <section> ---` headers and a compact skill summary instead of the raw `<available_skills>` XML:

```bash
poo prompt --pretty --profile reviewer
```

`poo prompt` honors `--settings`, `--profile`, `--project-prompt`, `--user-prompt-file`, `--system-prompt`, and `--append-system-prompt`, and works without a configured chat model.

---

<!-- Source: capabilities/feeds-and-daemon.md -->

# Feeds & Daemon

Most agent harnesses only move when a user types a prompt. `poo` can also run **feeds** — long-lived external commands or MCP resource subscriptions that push asynchronous inputs into a session as `feed:<name>`. Paired with `poo daemon`, a session becomes a durable, lease-backed resident process that sleeps while idle, wakes when something happens, and resumes across restarts.

## What feeds are

A feed is a source that runs beside a session and emits messages into it. Feeds come in two forms:

- **Command feeds** (declared in `feeds` manifests): long-lived processes started through the session's executor whose stdout carries one JSON message per line.
- **MCP resource feeds** (declared in `mcp.json`'s `poo` block): subscriptions to an MCP server's `resources/subscribe` URI that drain updates into the same delivery and filter pipeline. See [MCP Servers](/capabilities/mcp-servers) for server setup and relaunch behavior.

Every feed input is delivered to the model as untrusted outside input wrapped in a `<feed>` XML element:

```xml
<feed name="avenor-inbox" from="worker-1">Tests failed in pkg/auth; should I revert the fixture change?</feed>
```

- `name` is the feed's label: `<name>` for always-on or unscoped feeds, or `<name>[<field>=<value>]` for scoped optional subscriptions.
- `from` is omitted when the message has no sender.
- `&` and `<` are escaped in the text body (and `"`, `\n`, `\r` in attributes) so payload content cannot close the element.
- Lifecycle transitions are recorded as `feed.started` and `feed.ended` in the [session log](/reference/session-log-v0).

### Command feed stdout protocol

A command feed writes one JSON object per line to stdout:

```json
{"text": "PR #42 has a new review comment.", "from": "alice"}
```

A message may attach an image beside its text, or send an image alone with `text` omitted:

```json
{"text": "Build dashboard snapshot", "image": {"path": "shot.png", "media": "image/png"}}
```

Protocol rules:

- `text` is required unless `image` is present. `from` is optional; `id` is reserved and ignored; unknown fields are ignored; blank lines are skipped.
- Maximum line length is **1 MiB**.
- `image.path` is required (relative paths resolve against the feed command's working directory). `image.media` is optional; when present, the file's magic bytes must match it. Images are capped at **5 MB** and refused if unreadable, mismatched, oversized, or if the session's model does not accept image input.
- Protocol violations fail the attempt immediately, including malformed JSON, lines over 1 MiB, missing text or image, and refused inputs. `poo` stops the command, discards remaining output, and reaps the process.
- Stderr is written to the session's structured log (up to **64 KiB** per attempt) and never shown to the model.

## Feed manifests

Feed manifests are JSON, YAML (`.yaml`/`.yml`), or TOML (`.toml`) files loaded from `feeds.paths`, `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/poo/feeds/` (unless disabled), `POO_FEEDS_PATH`, and `--feeds-path`.

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "feeds": {
    "inbox": {
      "description": "Messages from the team queue.",
      "command": ["my-cli", "inbox"],
      "env": {
        "QUEUE_URL": "env:QUEUE_URL",
        "SESSION_ID": "session:id",
        "QUEUE_MODE": "batch"
      },
      "restart": true,
      "on_idle": "wake",
      "max_pending": 32
    }
  }
}
```

Key fields:

- `version`: must be `1`.
- Feed name: matches `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*$` and must be unique across all loaded feed manifests and MCP resource feeds.
- `command`: required argv array.
- `description`: rendered in the jobs prompt so the model knows what each feed provides.
- `env`: added on top of the CLI registry's benign environment variables (never inheriting variables scrubbed by `tools.env.scrub`). Values may be literals, `env:NAME` (from the scrubbed host environment), `session:id` (the session's native ID, preserved across resumes), or `scope:NAME` (for optional feeds). Unresolved references fail the attempt before the command starts.
- `max_pending`: caps undelivered queued inputs for the feed (default `16`). Past the cap, the oldest undelivered input is dropped unread.

See the [Manifests Reference](/reference/manifests#feed-manifests) for the complete schema and validation rules.

## Restart policy

Set `"restart": true` to restart a command feed after its process exits or hits a protocol failure:

- Backoff starts at **1s** and doubles on each consecutive exit or failure, capped at **60s**.
- An attempt that stays up for **60s or longer** resets the backoff timer.
- `cancel_job` and session close always cancel any pending restart.
- **Exception:** if a [command filter](#command-filter-external-script) fails, the feed is **suspended** and does not restart regardless of `restart`.

## Idle wake behavior

`on_idle` controls whether a feed input can start a new run when the session is idle:

| `on_idle` | Behavior when session is idle |
|---|---|
| `wake` | Starts a new run to handle the incoming feed message. |
| `hold` | Queues the message until a run is already active. |
| *(omitted)* | Inherits `jobs.on_idle` for always-on feeds; defaults to `hold` for `optional: true` feeds. |

Whenever a run starts (from a `wake` feed, a background job, or client input), it drains all queued inputs — including held ones.

To guard against runaway autonomous loops, set `jobs.max_unattended_wakes` in settings to cap consecutive woken runs with no client input in between (`0` disables the cap).

## Optional feeds (`subscribe_feed` and `cancel_job`)

A feed marked `"optional": true` does not start when the session opens. Instead, the model starts instances on demand with `subscribe_feed` and stops them with `cancel_job`.

Optional feeds can declare a `scope` — string fields (with optional regex `pattern`s) that the model supplies when subscribing and that bind into `env` via `scope:<field>`:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "feeds": {
    "git-feedback": {
      "description": "Feedback on one repository's pull requests.",
      "command": ["git-feedback", "--watch"],
      "optional": true,
      "scope": {
        "url": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^https://"}
      },
      "env": {
        "GIT_FEEDBACK_URL": "scope:url"
      },
      "on_idle": "wake",
      "restart": true
    }
  }
}
```

How subscriptions work:

- **Starting an instance:** the model calls `subscribe_feed` with `{"feed": "git-feedback", "scope": {"url": "https://github.com/org/repo"}}`. Scope values are validated against the manifest schema; missing fields, unknown fields, or pattern mismatches are returned as tool refusals.
- **Origin and job ID:** scoped instances are identified as `feed:<name>[<field>=<value>]` with fields sorted by name and values query-escaped (e.g., `feed:git-feedback[url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Forg%2Frepo]`). Unscoped optional feeds use `feed:<name>`.
- **Idempotency:** subscribing to the same feed and scope reaches the existing instance instead of starting a duplicate. If the instance was stopped or suspended, `subscribe_feed` starts it again.
- **Instance cap:** a session runs at most **8** feed instances at once (counting running, restarting, and suspended instances). A ninth distinct subscription is refused until one is stopped with `cancel_job`.
- **Inspecting and stopping:** `jobs` lists all running and suspended feeds with tool type `feed`. `cancel_job` accepts the feed's job ID (`feed:<name>` or `feed:<name>[...]`) and stops it. See [Built-in Tools & Jobs](/capabilities/tools-and-jobs).
- **Reload behavior:** when a session reloads, always-on feeds start automatically. **Durable** sessions also restore active optional subscriptions from the session log; **logged** sessions do not (the model must call `subscribe_feed` again).

## Filtering before delivery

A feed's `filter` block screens records before they enter the session queue. A manifest may configure either a **question filter** or a **command filter**, never both.

### Question filter (decision model)

A question filter asks the session's [decision model](/capabilities/decision-model) a yes/no question about each message's text:

```json
"filter": {
  "question": "Does this event report a failed required check or an unclear status?",
  "min_no_probability": 0.95
}
```

- Phrase `question` so **yes** means deliver. `min_no_probability` must be `> 0.5` and `<= 1`.
- The decider sees only the feed name, sender, and message text — never the conversation history.
- A message is dropped only when `P(no)` (multiplied by label mass, if the endpoint reports one) meets or exceeds `min_no_probability`. Dropped messages never enter the queue and cannot wake an idle session.
- **Fails open:** messages pass through unfiltered when screening cannot run. This includes sessions with no decision model (warns once), failed calls, or calls exceeding the **1.5s** budget. Image-only messages and messages whose sender plus text exceeds **8 KiB** also pass through.

**Runtime question override:** `subscribe_feed` accepts an optional `prompt` to set or replace a feed instance's question without restarting it. It also accepts an optional `min_no_probability`, defaulting to the manifest's threshold or `0.6`. Passing an empty `prompt` clears the override and restores the manifest's question. Setting a `prompt` is refused if the feed uses a command filter or if the session has no decision model.

### Command filter (external script)

A command filter runs an external command once per source record, transforming or dropping it before delivery:

```json
"filter": {
  "command": ["/path/to/excerpt", "--max", "2000"]
}
```

- The source JSON record is written to the filter's stdin.
- The filter writes a stream of JSON record objects to stdout (compact or pretty-printed). Empty stdout drops the record; multiple objects fan one source record out into multiple inputs.
- Output records accept `text`, `from`, `image`, and an optional structured `data` object (only command-filtered feeds carry `data`).
- Runs under the same executor, working directory, and environment as the feed command.
- Caps: **1 MiB** per record on input and output, and at most **4 MiB** and **256 records** per filter invocation.
- **Fails closed:** a nonzero exit, invalid JSON output, or exceeding any cap fails the attempt and **suspends** the feed (ignoring `restart`). `poo` writes filter diagnostics to a log file beside the session and wakes the session with a fault report (`<feed fault="..." log="...">`). Optional feeds can be restarted with `subscribe_feed`; always-on and MCP resource feeds remain suspended until session close or resume.

## Profile feed declarations and `feeds.defaults`

- **`feeds.defaults`** (default `true`): controls whether `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/poo/feeds/` loads automatically alongside `feeds.paths`. A profile's `feeds_defaults` overrides `feeds.defaults` and is inherited from its `base` profile. See [Manifests Reference](/reference/manifests#defaults-and-profile-interaction).
- **`profiles.<name>.feeds`**: declares feed names that a profile expects to be present (inherited and merged from `base`). This is a **presence assertion**, not a switch — `feeds.paths` and defaults still decide what loads, and an MCP resource feed satisfies the name as well. If a declared feed is not loaded, `poo` emits a warning rather than failing the build. See [Profiles & Prompts](/configuration/profiles-and-prompts).

## `poo daemon`

`poo daemon` hosts a long-lived, feed-driven session without reading stdin. It is designed to run under a supervisor (`systemd`, `launchd`, a container entrypoint, or a background terminal) and keep a session alive across restarts.

```sh
poo daemon --session ops-inbox --working-dir /srv/app
```

Key behaviors:

- **Durable by default:** unless `--session-mode` or `session.mode` is set, `poo daemon` selects `durable` mode so runs, pending inputs, and optional feed subscriptions survive crashes. See [Sessions & Durability](/operations/sessions-and-durability).
- **Lease-backed ownership:** the daemon acquires the session's lease (or takes it over if the previous owner died). If another owner takes over the lease while the daemon is running, `poo daemon` exits immediately with code `1` rather than writing into another owner's session.
- **No wire client:** permission asks cannot prompt an interactive user; the asker chain is `[decide]` (active only when a decision model is configured).
- **Clean shutdown:** `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM` stops feeds, flushes session records, releases the lease, and exits `0`.

### Flags

In addition to shared and endpoint flags (`--settings`, `--profile`, `--feeds-path`, `--mcp-path`, `--cli-registry-path`, etc.):

| Flag | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--session <id>` | generated ID | Session ID to load (taking over a dead owner's lease) or create if it does not exist. |
| `--auto-resume` | `true` | Resume an unsettled pending run on load. Overrides `session.durable.auto_resume`. |
| `--working-dir <dir>` | current dir | Working directory for the session's tools and feeds. |

### Lifecycle stderr

`poo daemon` logs one lifecycle fact per line to stderr:

```text
poo daemon: started
poo daemon: session ops-inbox
poo daemon: 1 feed(s)
poo daemon: idle
```

When taking over a session with an unsettled run:

```text
poo daemon: started
poo daemon: session ops-inbox
poo daemon: 1 feed(s)
poo daemon: the session was taken over: a run was left unsettled
poo daemon: resumed run_01J...
```

On shutdown or lease loss:

- `poo daemon: shutdown` (on `SIGINT` / `SIGTERM`)
- `poo daemon: the lease was lost: a takeover owner now holds the session`

### Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | Clean shutdown after `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM`. |
| `1` | Operational failure: store open/create/resume error, failed pending-run resume, broken session, or lost lease. |
| `2` | Usage or configuration error: invalid flags, bad working directory, invalid settings, or invalid session ID. |

See [Limits & Exit Codes](/operations/limits-and-exit-codes) for exit codes across all `poo` subcommands.

## End-to-end example

This example wires an Avenor inbox feed and CLI delegation tools into a durable daemon session that wakes whenever a child agent sends a question.

**1. Feed manifest (`feeds.json`):**

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "feeds": {
    "avenor-inbox": {
      "description": "Receive Avenor messages",
      "command": ["avenor", "feed", "broker"],
      "env": {
        "AVENOR_BIND_HOST": "poo",
        "AVENOR_BIND_SESSION": "session:id"
      },
      "on_idle": "wake",
      "restart": true
    }
  }
}
```

**2. Settings (`settings.yaml`):**

```yaml
feeds:
  defaults: false
  paths: [./feeds.json]

cli_registry:
  defaults: false
  paths: [./examples/avenor/tools.json]

jobs:
  max_unattended_wakes: 10

session:
  mode: durable
  durable:
    lease_ttl_s: 30
```

**3. Start the daemon:**

```sh
poo daemon --settings settings.yaml --session avenor-coordinator
```

`poo daemon` prints its startup lines to stderr, starts `avenor feed broker` with `AVENOR_BIND_SESSION=avenor-coordinator`, and waits idle:

```text
poo daemon: started
poo daemon: session avenor-coordinator
poo daemon: 1 feed(s)
poo daemon: idle
```

When `avenor feed broker` prints a JSON line to stdout, `poo` wakes the idle session and delivers `<feed name="avenor-inbox" ...>` to the model. The model can then reply via its registered tools. If the daemon is stopped with `SIGTERM` and started again with `--session avenor-coordinator`, it reattaches to the same session ID, restarts `avenor-inbox`, and resumes any unsettled run.

---

<!-- Source: capabilities/compaction.md -->

# Context Compaction

Long sessions eventually exceed a model's context window or an endpoint's prompt limit. `poo` handles this through pluggable **compaction strategies** configured under `context.strategy` (default: `mine`).

## Transparent history

Compaction in `poo` changes only the **view** sent to the model — never what the session recorded.

- **Nothing is rewritten silently.** Every replacement starts with a visible marker (`[Context compacted: turns 1-N reconstructed below]` or `[Context compacted: turns 1-N summarized below]`), provider windows append `[context compacted by provider]`, and tool-result rewrites preserve their handle with a compacted marker.
- **The store stays whole.** Every original turn and tool result remains in the session log intact and recoverable.
- **Retention pointers and file lists.** Replacement strategies append a list of files touched in the covered turns (`read`, `edit`, `write`). This keeps the model from re-reading those files. `mine` and `pointer` also append a retention pointer with the session ID and replaced turn range. When enabled, it names the `history` tool to search or read those turns back on demand.
- **One form per compaction.** Core validates every compaction before applying it. A compaction takes exactly one of four forms: a turn-range replacement (`Replace`), a tool-result rewrite (`Rewrite`), a provider-native window (`Window`), or a run-ending handoff (`End`). If a compaction fails or is rejected, the run continues uncompacted when the next request still fits, or settles with `context_exhausted` when it does not.

See [Sessions & Durability](/operations/sessions-and-durability) for how session logs are persisted and replayed.

## When compaction fires (the fit rule)

Every strategy compacts when the next request no longer fits its budget. `poo` tracks two limits from the active model's metadata (see [Models & Catalog](/configuration/models-and-catalog)):

- **`context_limit`** — the model's total context window (prompt + output).
- **`input_limit`** — the largest prompt the endpoint accepts, if lower than `context_limit`.

The effective prompt ceiling (`PromptLimit`) is the smaller of the two (ignoring whichever is unset). After at least one turn has been sent, the fit rule triggers when either condition holds:

1. **Window room is short:** `estimated_input + output_need + 256 > context_limit`
2. **Input cap is exceeded:** `estimated_input + 256 > input_limit`

Where `256` is the fixed token reserve (`OutputReserve`), and `output_need` is the larger of the run's `OutputLimit` and the strategy's fork output limit (for strategies that fork: `mine`, `pointer`, and `handoff`). Because a fork re-sends the whole current window, its output limit counts toward the fit rule.

Additional guards:

- **Over-window start:** Block strategies (`mine`, `pointer`, `summary`) also fire immediately, even before a turn completes. They trigger if the view leaves under `256` tokens of output room (`MinOutputTokens`) or exceeds `input_limit`.
- **At least two live turns:** Block strategies never compact a single live turn; there must be older turns behind the active work.
- **Must restore room:** Block strategies check whether the replacement (plus its marker, file list, and retention pointer) would actually end the shortage. On a window too small for the verbatim tail plus replacement to recover room, compaction is skipped rather than looping every turn. Similarly, `native` declines to repeat if the provider's last compacted input already left the window short, letting the request gate settle `no_output_room`.
- **Small-window tail cap:** The verbatim tail (`keep_recent_tokens`) is automatically capped at 50% of `PromptLimit` so small-window models can still compact.

### Optional early trigger (`ratio`)

Setting `ratio` (a float between `0` and `1`) under `context.mine`, `context.pointer`, `context.summary`, or `context.handoff` adds an earlier trigger when `estimated_input >= ratio * PromptLimit` (after at least one turn). When unset, the fit rule alone decides.

::: warning Removed keys: `notice_ratio` and `hard_ratio`
`context.notice_ratio` and `context.hard_ratio` have been removed and have no effect. A settings file that still sets them loads with a warning. Use the fit rule (default) or a strategy-specific `ratio` instead.
:::

## Strategy comparison

| Strategy | How it works | When to use | Requirements | Trade-offs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mine` *(default)* | Forks the chat model for advisory pointers, then reads the covered transcript in a fresh request to reconstruct task-shaped working context. | General-purpose long sessions where task state matters more than chronological order. | Model must handle two side requests (fork + ask). | Higher compaction token cost (reads covered transcript); best fidelity for complex work. |
| `pointer` | Forks the chat model for JSON search queries and notes. Runs literal searches over retained history and composes context from matches and seed without reading the full transcript. | Very long sessions or when using a smaller-window `roles.compaction` model. | Readable session history for query extraction; falls back to `mine` on failure. | Bounded compose input; can miss unqueried details (recoverable via `history` tool). |
| `summary` | Single fresh request reads the covered turns and writes a structured chronological checkpoint. | Conventional summarization with a smaller output budget and no fork pass. | Model must handle one side request (ask). | No fork pass and no retention pointer; chronological summary can lose non-linear details. |
| `handoff` | Forks the chat model to write a continuation note, then ends the run (`context_exhausted`) with the handoff text. | Orchestrators that prefer starting fresh sessions from an explicit handoff rather than mutating history. | Caller must handle `context_exhausted` and seed a new session. | Terminates the run; does not continue in-place. |
| `native` | Asks the provider's own compaction endpoint to produce an opaque compacted window and installs it as the view. | When using a provider that supports server-side state compaction. | Model declares `ops: [chat, compact]` and uses a transport implementing `NativeCompactor` (currently `openai-codex`). | Provider-locked; opaque state cannot be transferred across models or providers. |
| `none` | Disables compaction completely. | Short runs, benchmarks, or callers managing context externally. | None. | Run settles `context_exhausted` (`no_output_room` or `prompt_limit`) once the window fills. |

## Strategies in detail

### `mine` (default)

`context.strategy: mine` reconstructs the covered turns into a task-shaped working context using two requests:

1. **Pointer pass (fork):** Re-sends the last main request on `roles.chat` and asks what the replacement must preserve (turns, file paths, error strings, open threads). The pass is best-effort: if the fork fails, is truncated, or returns a tool call, `mine` proceeds without pointers because the transcript still holds everything.
2. **Mining pass (ask):** Sends the covered transcript, any prior replacement, and the fork's pointers to `roles.compaction` (or `roles.chat` if unset). Tool results are capped and reasoning blocks are stripped. A truncated reply or tool call is rejected rather than installed.

The replacement includes the marker line, the reconstruction, a list of read/modified files, and a retention pointer naming the session and replaced turns.

```yaml
context:
  strategy: mine
  mine:
    # ratio: 0.85            # optional early trigger; fit rule decides when unset
    keep_recent_tokens: 12000 # default: 12000
    max_tokens: 32768         # default: 32768
    # pointer_max_tokens: 16384 # optional; defaults to window-scaled output limit
```

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ratio` | unset (`0`) | Optional share of `PromptLimit` for an early trigger. |
| `keep_recent_tokens` | `12000` | Tokens of newest history kept verbatim (capped at 50% of `PromptLimit`). |
| `max_tokens` | `32768` | Output token limit for the mining request. |
| `pointer_max_tokens` | window-scaled | Output token limit for the fork pass. Defaults to `8192` (`< 64k` window), `16384` (`64k–128k` or unknown), or `32768` (`>= 128k`). |

### `pointer`

`context.strategy: pointer` keeps `mine`'s fork but makes the pointers load-bearing so the covered transcript is never read whole:

1. **Pointer pass (fork):** Asks the chat model for a JSON object of literal search `queries` (capped at 8) and `notes`. Requests JSON response format when supported; if the endpoint refuses the parameter, retries once without it. Replies are parsed leniently. If malformed prose returns, a small reformat ask on `roles.compaction` tries to recover JSON before treating the text as `notes`.
2. **Extraction:** Runs each query as a literal search (`regexp.QuoteMeta`) over the store's retained history, deduplicating matches up to `snippet_budget` bytes (cut cleanly on UTF-8 rune boundaries).
3. **Compose pass (ask):** Sends only the orientation seed (the last three non-empty user messages), extracted snippets, notes, and any prior replacement to `roles.compaction`. Because the full transcript is never sent, the compaction model's window bounds only the compose request, not the session's total size.

**Fallback to `mine`:** If the compose request fails, hits `max_tokens`, returns a tool call, or returns empty text, `pointer` falls back to `mine` with the same `ratio`, `keep_recent_tokens`, `max_tokens`, and `pointer_max_tokens`. If `escalate_after` is set to a positive integer `N`, once the session has run `N` compactions, all subsequent compactions delegate directly to the full-span `mine` fallback.

```yaml
context:
  strategy: pointer
  pointer:
    # ratio: 0.85            # optional early trigger; fit rule decides when unset
    keep_recent_tokens: 12000 # default: 12000
    max_tokens: 32768         # default: 32768
    # pointer_max_tokens: 16384 # optional; defaults to window-scaled output limit
    snippet_budget: 32768     # default: 32768 (bytes)
    # escalate_after: 3       # optional; default 0 (never escalate)
```

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ratio` | unset (`0`) | Optional share of `PromptLimit` for an early trigger. |
| `keep_recent_tokens` | `12000` | Tokens of newest history kept verbatim. |
| `max_tokens` | `32768` | Output token limit for the compose request. |
| `pointer_max_tokens` | window-scaled | Output token limit for the fork (and reform) pass. Same window scaling as `mine`. |
| `snippet_budget` | `32768` | Maximum total bytes of retained-history snippets collected across queries. |
| `escalate_after` | `0` (off) | Number of compactions a session runs before delegating all later compactions to `mine`. |

### `summary`

`context.strategy: summary` is the conventional single-request checkpoint strategy. It skips the fork pass and sends covered turns (plus any prior summary) to `roles.compaction` (or `roles.chat`). It replaces those turns with the summary, marker line, and file list, without a retention pointer.

```yaml
context:
  strategy: summary
  summary:
    # ratio: 0.85            # optional early trigger; fit rule decides when unset
    keep_recent_tokens: 20000 # default: 20000
    max_tokens: 4096          # default: 4096
```

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ratio` | unset (`0`) | Optional share of `PromptLimit` for an early trigger. |
| `keep_recent_tokens` | `20000` | Tokens of newest history kept verbatim. |
| `max_tokens` | `4096` | Output token limit for the summarization request. |

### `handoff`

`context.strategy: handoff` refuses to compact in-place. When triggered, it forks the last main request on `roles.chat` and asks the model for a handoff note. It then ends the run with `context_exhausted`, carrying that note in the settle detail. A truncated or empty reply is rejected. The caller can then seed a fresh session with the handoff note.

```yaml
context:
  strategy: handoff
  handoff:
    # ratio: 0.85   # optional early trigger; fit rule decides when unset
    max_tokens: 2048 # default: 2048
```

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ratio` | unset (`0`) | Optional share of `PromptLimit` for an early trigger. |
| `max_tokens` | `2048` | Output token limit for the handoff fork request. |

### `native`

`context.strategy: native` asks the provider's transport to compact its own conversation state and installs the returned provider window (followed by `[context compacted by provider]`) as the model's view. System instructions remain intact.

`native` is opt-in and has strict capability checks:

- The active model must declare `compact` in its `ops` list (`ops: [chat, compact]`).
- Its transport must implement `NativeCompactor`. In this repository, only the `openai-codex` Responses transport implements native compaction.
- Settings validation refuses `context.strategy: native` on unsupported transports such as Chat Completions. Mid-session model switches are re-checked when compaction runs: switching to a model without `ops: [..., compact]` refuses native compaction rather than calling an incapable provider.

```yaml
models:
  openai-codex/gpt-6.1-sol:
    endpoint: openai-codex
    model_id: gpt-6.1-sol
    api: responses
    ops: [chat, compact]
roles:
  chat: openai-codex/gpt-6.1-sol
context:
  strategy: native
```

`native` exposes no `context.native` sub-keys in settings; it triggers strictly on the fit rule.

### `none`

`context.strategy: none` disables compaction. The session runs until the request gate blocks a request for `no_output_room` or `prompt_limit`, settling the run with `context_exhausted`.

```yaml
context:
  strategy: none
```

## The `compaction` role

`roles.compaction` assigns a dedicated model to a strategy's own standalone requests (`Ask`), defaulting to `roles.chat` when unset (see [Roles and Required Operations](/configuration/models-and-catalog#roles-and-required-operations)):

```yaml
roles:
  chat: openai-codex/gpt-6.1-sol
  compaction: opencode-go/glm-5.3
```

- **What moves to `roles.compaction`:** The summarization request (`summary`), the mining request (`mine`), and the compose and reformat requests (`pointer`). The model must serve the `chat` operation and is built through the same catalog and transport machinery as other roles.
- **Why the fork stays on `roles.chat`:** The pointer pass (`mine`, `pointer`) and handoff pass (`handoff`) fork the last main request byte-for-byte with appended instructions. Only the chat model's transport can reuse that cached prefix and see the exact window the chat model just worked in. Forks therefore always run on `roles.chat`.

## Related pages

- [Settings Reference](/reference/settings) — complete schema for `context.*` and `roles.compaction`
- [Models & Catalog](/configuration/models-and-catalog) — configuring `context_limit`, `input_limit`, `max_output`, and `ops`
- [Sessions & Durability](/operations/sessions-and-durability) — session log retention and replay
- [Limits & Exit Codes](/operations/limits-and-exit-codes) — `context_exhausted`, `no_output_room`, and `prompt_limit`
- [Built-in Tools & Jobs](/capabilities/tools-and-jobs) — the `history` tool for reading retained turns

# Decision Model

`poo` supports a dedicated **decision model** (`roles.decider`) alongside the chat model (see [Roles and Required Operations](/configuration/models-and-catalog#roles-and-required-operations)). Instead of free-form prose, it takes a state payload and typed questions and returns a probability distribution over the allowed answers. Questions can be `Bool` (yes/no), `Choice` (up to 26 named options), or `Score` (2 to 10 levels).

Every call through a session's decider is wrapped by `decide.Recorded` (`poo/decide`), which writes a `decision` record to the [session log](/reference/session-log-v0). Each record includes the caller origin, `state_hash`, questions, answers, outcome (`ok`, `deferred`, or `invalid`), latency, and wire request count.

## Configuring `roles.decider`

A model assigned to `roles.decider` must declare `ops: [systemone]` (or `decisions`). Models that serve only chat turns are rejected at construction time.

### Built-in TypeSafe provider

`poo` ships a built-in `typesafe` decisions provider (`https://api.typesafe.ai/v1`) serving `typesafe/jev-latest` and `typesafe/jev-preview`. Jev answers decision questions only and serves no chat turns.

Authenticate with `poo login typesafe` or set `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in the environment (see [Providers & Auth](/configuration/providers-and-auth)), then assign the role:

```yaml
roles:
  chat: opencode-go/glm-5.3
  decider: typesafe/jev-latest

decider:
  timeout_ms: 1500
```

The TypeSafe endpoint rejects a request-level `instructions` field and has no OpenAI-shaped `/models` list. Its built-in definition therefore sets `instructions_per_question: true` (folding call framing into each question) and `skip_probe: true`.

### Custom decision endpoints and models

To point `roles.decider` at a newer TypeSafe model or a self-hosted `systemone`-compatible endpoint, declare the endpoint and model with `ops: [systemone]`:

```yaml
endpoints:
  my-decider:
    endpoint: https://api.typesafe.ai/v1
    api_key_env: TYPESAFE_API_KEY
    skip_probe: true
    instructions_per_question: true

models:
  my-decider/jev-next:
    endpoint: my-decider
    model_id: jev-next
    ops: [systemone]
    inputs: [text]
    context_limit: 64000

roles:
  chat: opencode-go/glm-5.3
  decider: my-decider/jev-next
```

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `roles.decider` | string | unset | Model name (`provider/model`) for the decider role. Must serve `systemone` or `decisions`. |
| `decider.timeout_ms` | int | unset | Global per-call latency budget in milliseconds (minimum `1` when set). |
| `endpoints.<name>.instructions_per_question` | bool | `false` | Fold request-level framing into each question for endpoints that reject a top-level `instructions` field. |
| `models.<name>.ops` | string[] | `[]` | Operations served by the model; include `systemone` for decision models. |

## Where `poo` uses the decision model

Today, three built-in subsystems call `roles.decider` when it is configured.

::: info Growing surface
This subsystem set is not the end of the road. `poo` is under active development, and more decision-backed capabilities, integrations, and hooks will be added over time. Custom Go binaries can also call `poo/decide.Decider` directly from their own [hooks](/extending/architecture).
:::

### 1. Permission asker (`perm/decide`)

The `decide` permission asker (`poo/perm/decide`) sits in the [permission asker chain](/operations/permissions-and-safety) to judge unmatched side-effecting tool calls automatically.

When asked, it sends one `Bool` question (`allow`) along with a bounded evidence payload framed as data, not instructions:

- Up to 20 recent conversation turns (`DefaultEvidenceTurns`), with message text capped at 512 chars, tool inputs at 256 chars, and tool outputs at 512 chars.
- The working directory and the pending call's tool name, summary, class, reason, and permitted arguments.

The asker compares the returned probabilities against two thresholds:

- `P(yes) >= permission.decide.allow` → **allow** (default `0.85`).
- `P(no) >= permission.decide.deny` → **deny** (default `0.99`).
- Anything in between — as well as timeouts, errors, panics, or invalid probability distributions — **defers** to the next asker in `permission.askers` (or `permission.fallback`). A deferral never grants permission.

```yaml
roles:
  chat: opencode-go/glm-5.3
  decider: typesafe/jev-latest

permission:
  askers: [decide, wire]
  fallback: deny
  decide:
    allow: 0.85
    deny: 0.99
    timeout_ms: 1500
```

Setting `decide` in `permission.askers` or configuring any `permission.decide.*` key requires `roles.decider` to be set.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `permission.decide.allow` | float | `0.85` | Minimum `yes` probability (`0`–`1`) to allow a call. |
| `permission.decide.deny` | float | `0.99` | Minimum `no` probability (`0`–`1`) to deny a call. |
| `permission.decide.timeout_ms` | int | `1500` | Per-call latency budget for the permission asker, in milliseconds. |

### 2. Feed record filtering

A [feed manifest](/capabilities/feeds-and-daemon) can declare a question `filter` to screen incoming messages before they enter the session. The model can also set one dynamically on a running feed:

```yaml
filter:
  question: "Is this message actionable for the active repository?"
  min_no_probability: 0.8
```

For each emitted record, `poo` asks the decision model one `Bool` question (`yes` = deliver, `no` = drop) over `{ feed, from, text }` with a `1500ms` timeout and an 8 KiB combined sender+text limit. A message is dropped only when `P(no)` (multiplied by `label_mass` if reported) is at least `min_no_probability` (valid range `(0.5, 1]`; default `0.6` for model-set prompts).

Question filters **fail open** and deliver messages unfiltered when screening cannot run. That includes sessions with no decider (logged once per feed attempt), image-only messages, and payloads over 8 KiB. Messages also pass through when the decider times out or defers.

### 3. Large CLI and MCP catalog search (`find_tool`)

Sessions with [CLI Registry](/capabilities/cli-registry) manifests and [MCP servers](/capabilities/mcp-servers) can accumulate dozens or hundreds of entries. When the catalog exceeds 30 entries (`cli.FindThreshold`) and a decision model is configured, `poo` offers `find_tool` instead of dumping the full catalog into the system prompt.

When the model calls `find_tool` with a natural-language `intent`, `poo` asks the decision model one `Bool` question per offered entry. Requests batch up to 64 questions each, with up to 4 requests in flight. `find_tool` returns the top 8 matching entries ranked best-first with their schemas. If the search fails or the decider is unavailable, `find_tool` returns a short notice instead of dumping the catalog.

---

<!-- Source: capabilities/cli-registry.md -->

# CLI Registry & Script Tools

You do not need to build a custom Go binary to give `poo` new tools. Drop a JSON manifest into `~/.config/poo/cli-registry/`, or point `cli_registry.paths` at a manifest directory. `poo` compiles the argument schema and validates calls before starting a process. It then runs the command through the session's executor, sandbox, permissions, and background jobs.

The manifest format is powered by `github.com/sdougbrown/cli-registry` (`poo/cli` and `poo/tool/cliregistry`).

## Walkthrough: wrapping a CLI without recompiling

Suppose you have `writetighter` on `PATH` and want the model to lint prose with `writetighter lint`. Create a manifest at `~/.config/poo/cli-registry/writetighter.json`:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "tools": {
    "tighten-lint": {
      "description": "Run writetighter lint on a file or directory to catch prose issues.",
      "command": ["writetighter", "lint"],
      "inputSchema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "path": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "File or directory to lint."
          },
          "kind": {
            "type": "string",
            "enum": ["pr", "plan", "doc", "commit"],
            "description": "Document kind for rule selection."
          }
        },
        "required": ["path"],
        "additionalProperties": false
      },
      "bindings": [
        {
          "property": "kind",
          "style": "space",
          "flag": "--kind"
        },
        {
          "property": "path",
          "style": "positional"
        }
      ],
      "output": {
        "mode": "raw"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Start a session with a side-effecting profile (such as `code`):

- Because the manifest sits in `~/.config/poo/cli-registry/`, `poo` loads it automatically with no settings change.
- Because the catalog has 30 or fewer entries, `tighten-lint` is promoted to a direct tool: the model calls `tighten-lint({"path": "docs/README.md", "kind": "doc"})` directly.
- `poo` validates the arguments against `inputSchema` before spawning a process, builds `["writetighter", "lint", "--kind", "doc", "--", "docs/README.md"]`, and runs it through the session's executor.

::: tip Protecting flag-like values
Separate-value flag bindings (`style: "space"`) reject values that start with `-` at validation time so a model cannot inject extra flags. `equals` bindings (`--flag=value`) stay inside a single argv element, and `positional` bindings are separated with `--`.
:::

## Manifest discovery and `cli_registry.defaults`

`poo` loads manifests from two sources, in order:

1. **Default user directory**: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/poo/cli-registry/` (typically `~/.config/poo/cli-registry/`). A missing directory is ignored.
2. **Configured paths**: `cli_registry.paths` in settings, plus any paths added by `POO_CLI_REGISTRY_PATH` (OS path-list separated) or repeatable `--cli-registry-path` flags on `poo run`, `poo serve`, and `poo prompt`.

Relative paths in `cli_registry.paths` resolve against the working directory; paths starting with `~/` resolve under the home directory. Duplicate tool names across two manifests fail the load and name both files.

```yaml
cli_registry:
  paths:
    - ./tools/registry
    - ~/shared-manifests/git.json
  defaults: true   # default; set false to ignore ~/.config/poo/cli-registry/
```

To isolate a project, binary, or test from ambient user manifests, set `cli_registry.defaults: false`. A profile can override that setting with `cli_registry_defaults`:

```yaml
cli_registry:
  defaults: false

profiles:
  personal:
    base: code
    cli_registry_defaults: true
```

## Direct tools vs. `call_cli` (the 30-entry threshold)

How registered entries appear to the model depends on the catalog size after availability filtering:

| Catalog size | Tools offered | Prompt catalog section |
|---|---|---|
| `1` to `30` entries | One direct tool per entry (manifest name + `inputSchema`) | None (the tool list already carries every schema) |
| `> 30` entries with a [decision model](/capabilities/decision-model) | `call_cli` + `find_tool` | Search guidance pointing to `find_tool` |
| `> 30` entries without a decision model | `call_cli` | Full catalog listing every entry and argument hint |

Both shapes execute through the exact same runner, executor, sandbox, timeout, environment resolution, and observation cap.

When behind `call_cli`, the model invokes an entry by name:

```json
{
  "command": "tighten-lint",
  "args": {
    "path": "docs/README.md",
    "kind": "doc"
  }
}
```

With a decision model configured, `find_tool` takes `{"intent": "..."}` and asks the decider one yes/no question per entry. It returns the top 8 matches with their argument schemas and dispatcher (`call_cli` or `call_mcp`).

### Collision behavior

Direct-tool promotion is **all or nothing**. The entire catalog stays behind `call_cli` instead of promoting if any of the following is true:

- The catalog has more than 30 entries.
- Any entry's name collides with a built-in/linked tool, a core tool (`jobs`, `cancel_job`, `subscribe_feed`, `finish`, `call_cli`, `find_tool`), or another tool the profile already offers. A manifest never shadows an existing tool.
- The profile explicitly names `call_cli` or `find_tool` itself.

::: info Reserved `background` argument
Direct tools support `background: true` by default. If a manifest's `inputSchema` already defines a property named `background`, that tool keeps its own argument and runs foreground-only rather than failing the session.
:::

## Disabling the registry

To turn off the CLI registry for a session or profile without deleting manifests, disable `call_cli`:

```yaml
tools:
  disabled: [call_cli]
```

Disabling `call_cli` suppresses both direct-tool promotion and `call_cli` itself.

## Availability gating (`profile_side_effecting`)

Without availability rules, `poo` offers the registry only to side-effecting profiles (such as `code`, not `search`). This default protects read-only profiles because arbitrary CLI commands can modify state.

Manifests can declare an Umpire `availability` block to gate entries per profile. `poo` supplies one boolean condition:

- `profile_side_effecting` (`boolean`): `true` when the profile offers any side-effecting tool, `false` for read-only profiles.

Once manifests declare `availability` conditions:

- Read-only profiles (such as `search`) earn the registry and receive only the entries whose rules leave them available.
- Profiles with no tools at all still receive no registry entries.
- Declaring any condition other than `profile_side_effecting`, or declaring `profile_side_effecting` as a type other than `boolean`, fails the build.

## Execution, environment, and permissions

Every registered command runs where `bash` runs:

- **Executor & sandbox**: Runs through the session's configured executor (local or [bubblewrap](/operations/sandbox)), in the session's working directory unless the manifest fixes a directory.
- **Environment**: Manifest `env` bindings accept literals, `env:NAME`, and `session:id`. `env:NAME` reads from the session's scrubbed environment, so variables removed by `tools.env.scrub` or excluded by `tools.env.passthrough` are unavailable. `session:id` resolves at call time to the session's ID and stays stable across resume. See [`examples/avenor/tools.json`](https://github.com/sdougbrown/poo/blob/main/examples/avenor/tools.json) for a multi-tool manifest using `session:id` and `stdin`/`equals`/`positional` bindings.
- **Permissions**: Registered tools are statically `side_effecting`. Behind `call_cli`, the primary argument is `command`, so [permission rules](/operations/permissions-and-safety) can match by command prefix. When promoted to direct tools, rules match by the tool's own name.
- **Background jobs**: Registered tools accept `background: true` and support `/bg` promotion in the REPL.

## Non-CLI JSON script tools

A registered tool does not have to wrap an existing CLI. Using a `json` stdin binding and `output.mode: "json"`, any script in any language becomes a typed tool:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "tools": {
    "sum_pair": {
      "description": "Sum a pair of numbers.",
      "command": ["python3", "fn_notes.py"],
      "inputSchema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "data": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
              "a": { "type": "number" },
              "b": { "type": "number" }
            },
            "required": ["a", "b"],
            "additionalProperties": false
          }
        },
        "required": ["data"],
        "additionalProperties": false
      },
      "bindings": [
        {
          "property": "data",
          "style": "json"
        }
      ],
      "output": {
        "mode": "json"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The contract is three rules:

1. **Stdin**: `style: "json"` serializes an object- or array-valued property as JSON onto the script's stdin. The bound property must be a concrete `object` or `array` in `inputSchema`, and a tool may have at most one `stdin` or `json` binding. An optional `flag` is emitted only when the property is present.
2. **Stdout**: `output.mode: "json"` parses the script's stdout as JSON and returns it directly as the tool result (bypassing the `bash` exit-code envelope). Any stderr written on a successful exit is appended after a newline.
3. **Errors**: A nonzero exit (outside `output.success_exit_codes`) returns a recoverable error envelope containing stdout, stderr, and the exit code.

::: warning `null` and over-cap JSON results
Two edge cases fall back to the standard exit-code envelope. This happens when stdout decodes to JSON `null`, or when the serialized result exceeds the observation cap. If a script can return an empty result, return an object such as `{"result": null}` instead of bare `null`.
:::

Non-CLI script tools join the exact same catalog, 30-entry promotion threshold, schema validation, permission policy (`side_effecting`), sandbox, and background job machinery as CLI entries. The `cli-registry` repository also ships a small Python helper (`helpers/python/poo_fn.py`) and runnable example (`examples/fn.json` + `examples/fn_notes.py`), though any executable that reads JSON from stdin and writes JSON to stdout works.

- [Built-in Tools & Jobs](/capabilities/tools-and-jobs) — built-in tools, observation caps, and background jobs
- [Manifests Reference](/reference/manifests) — full manifest schemas for CLI registry, feeds, and MCP
- [Build Your Own Binary](/extending/custom-binary) — when you actually want a custom Go binary with custom tools

# MCP Servers

`poo` runs Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers as session-owned stdio child processes. Loading an `mcp.json` manifest **declares** which servers exist; a profile's `mcp_servers` list **selects** which ones a session actually starts.

The model calls server tools through `call_mcp`, searches them beside CLI registry commands with `find_tool`, and can receive asynchronous messages from server resources through `poo` resource feeds.

## Loading `mcp.json` manifests

`poo` reads standard `mcp.json` files (the same `mcpServers` format used by Claude Code and other harnesses) from:

1. **Default user directory**: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/poo/mcp/` (typically `~/.config/poo/mcp/`), loaded when `mcp.defaults` is absent or `true`. A missing directory is not an error.
2. **Configured paths**: `mcp.paths` in settings (files or directories), plus `POO_MCP_PATH` (OS path-list separated) and repeatable `--mcp-path` flags on `poo run`, `poo serve`, and `poo prompt`.

Directories contribute their `.json` files and skip non-`.json` files; an explicit file path that is not `.json` fails the load. Relative paths resolve against the working directory; `~/` resolves under the home directory.

```yaml
mcp:
  paths:
    - examples/avenor-mcp
  defaults: false   # ignore ~/.config/poo/mcp/
```

A profile can override `mcp.defaults` with `mcp_defaults`.

### Manifest rules

- Top-level `mcpServers` is required. Each key is the server name (letters, digits, `-`, and `_`).
- `poo` reads `command` (required), `args`, `env`, `type`, and `url`. Other top-level keys and entry fields are ignored so one `mcp.json` can be shared across harnesses.
- Only `stdio` transport is supported. Entries with `type` set to `http`, `sse`, or `streamable-http` (or a `url` with no `type`) are skipped with a warning naming the server. Any other `type` value fails the load.
- Duplicate server names across files and duplicate JSON object keys within a file both fail the load.

## Profile opt-in (`mcp_servers`)

Loading a manifest starts nothing. A session starts only the servers named in its profile's `mcp_servers` list:

```yaml
profiles:
  avenor:
    base: code
    mcp_servers: [avenor]
profile: avenor
```

`mcp_servers` adds to the base profile's selection, deduplicated in order of first appearance. Selecting a server name that no loaded manifest defines produces a warning and skips it. A binary that does not link `call_mcp` fails the build if a profile selects any server.

### Process lifecycle and trust

- **Session-owned**: Each selected server starts when the session is created or resumed (with the session's ID and working directory) and stops when the session closes.
- **Startup budget**: Startup is bounded at **30 seconds** per server, including the MCP handshake and initial tool listing. A server that fails to start fails session creation or resume.
- **Unsandboxed host process**: MCP servers start directly on the host — not through the session's executor or sandbox — and run as the user running `poo`. They inherit the host environment minus `tools.env.scrub`, plus the manifest's resolved `env`. Select an MCP server with the same trust boundary as installing a program.

## Launch template variables

`command`, each element of `args`, and each `env` value support template expansion, resolved **at server launch** (not when settings load):

| Syntax | Resolution |
|---|---|
| `${NAME}` | Host environment variable `NAME`. Missing variable fails launch naming the server and variable. Can re-introduce a variable removed by `tools.env.scrub`. |
| `${NAME:-default}` | Host environment variable `NAME`, or `default` if unset. |
| `${session:id}` | The session's ID (stable across session resume). Cannot take a default. |
| `$$` | Literal `$`. |

Syntax errors — unterminated `${`, empty variable name, a default on `session:id`, or any `session:` variable other than `id` — fail manifest load.

## Calling tools: `call_mcp` and `find_tool`

The model reaches MCP tools through a single dispatcher, `call_mcp`, using `<server>/<tool>` qualified names:

```json
{
  "name": "avenor/spawn",
  "args": {
    "prompt": "Run the test suite and report failures.",
    "dir": "/path/to/repo"
  }
}
```

- **Permissions**: `call_mcp` is `side_effecting` and its primary argument is `name`. A [permission rule](/operations/permissions-and-safety) can allow or deny an entire server by prefix (for example `command_prefix: "avenor/"`) without listing individual tools.
- **Hints vs. permissions**: MCP tool annotations (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`) appear in the prompt catalog and `find_tool` results as `(read-only)` or `(destructive)` hints for the model. They never change the call's permission class.
- **Background jobs**: `call_mcp` supports `background: true` and `/bg` promotion in the REPL.
- **Outputs**: Text responses are elided in the middle if they exceed the observation cap. `structuredContent` rides along when it is valid JSON under the same cap (otherwise omitted with a note). Returned images become attachments when the active model accepts `image` input and the image fits within 5 MB. Otherwise, a note explains what was omitted.
- **Errors**: Unknown `<server>/<tool>` names are refused before calling. A stopped server returns `server <name> is down` as a recoverable error. A transport failure mid-call is reported and **never retried**, because the server may already have executed side effects.

### `find_tool` integration

When a session has a [decision model](/capabilities/decision-model):

- If the MCP offering exceeds 30 tools, the prompt points the model at `find_tool` instead of listing every tool inline.
- `find_tool` searches MCP tools and CLI registry commands together over a live snapshot of the session's offering. Each hit includes the tool's argument schema and tells the model which dispatcher (`call_mcp` or `call_cli`) and argument (`name` or `command`) to use.
- Because the snapshot is live, a down or relaunching server contributes no stale hits. Once it relaunches, its newly listed tools are immediately searchable.

## Resource feeds (`poo` block)

A manifest can include a top-level `poo` block to turn an MCP resource into a session feed. Unlike `mcpServers`, the `poo` block is **strict**: unknown fields fail the load.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "avenor": {
      "command": "avenor",
      "args": ["mcp", "--bind-host", "poo", "--bind-session", "${session:id}"]
    }
  },
  "poo": {
    "servers": {
      "avenor": {
        "feeds": {
          "avenor-inbox": {
            "resource": "avenor://inbox",
            "on_idle": "wake",
            "description": "Messages from Avenor children.",
            "filter": {
              "command": ["jq", "-c", ".text | fromjson | .messages[] | {from, text}"]
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Fields under `poo.servers.<server>.feeds.<feed>`:

- `resource` (required): Resource URI to subscribe to.
- `description`: Shown in the `jobs` prompt section.
- `on_idle`: `wake` or `hold` (inherits `jobs.on_idle` when omitted).
- `filter`: Optional [feed filter](/capabilities/feeds-and-daemon) using either `command` or `question`. A `command` filter fans one resource read into zero, one, or many inputs. A `question` filter screens each record with the decision model.

How resource feeds run:

- The server must advertise `resources/subscribe` in its handshake, or session creation fails.
- After subscribing, `poo` reads the resource once immediately (draining any backlog queued before subscription) and reads it again on each resource-updated notification.
- Each text content block is emitted as a record with the server name as `from` and the text verbatim (empty text and binary contents are skipped). Reads are drained at-most-once.
- Declared `command` filters run through the session's executor and working directory. Standard feed caps apply: 1 MiB per record, and 4 MiB or 256 records per filter run.
- Feed names must be lowercase letters, digits, `-`, and `_`, and must be unique across all MCP servers and configured command feeds. Two feeds cannot subscribe to the same server resource.
- Running resource feeds appear in `jobs` as `feed:<name>` and can be stopped with `cancel_job`.

## Bounded auto-relaunch

If a running MCP server exits unexpectedly during a session, `poo` relaunches it automatically:

- **Backoff**: First retry waits **1 second**, doubling on each consecutive failure up to **30 seconds**.
- **Reset**: A generation that stays up for at least **60 seconds** resets the failure counter.
- **Exhaustion**: After **5 consecutive failures**, the server is marked down for the remainder of the session:
  - `call_mcp` calls to that server return `server <name> is down`.
  - Any resource feeds attached to that server suspend with fault `filter_exited` (`server <name> stopped after 5 relaunches`).
  - The session itself keeps running; resuming the session starts with a fresh relaunch budget.
- **Re-sync**: On a successful relaunch, `poo` re-lists the server's tools (updating `call_mcp` and `find_tool` live; the initial prompt catalog is not re-rendered) and re-subscribes its resource feeds.

## Example: Avenor over MCP

The repository includes a complete working example in [`examples/avenor-mcp/`](https://github.com/sdougbrown/poo/tree/main/examples/avenor-mcp):

- [`examples/avenor-mcp/mcp.json`](https://github.com/sdougbrown/poo/blob/main/examples/avenor-mcp/mcp.json) launches `avenor mcp --bind-host poo --bind-session ${session:id}` and subscribes to `avenor://inbox` with a `jq` filter that fans out batched messages and attaches reply instructions for asks.
- [`examples/avenor-mcp/settings.yaml`](https://github.com/sdougbrown/poo/blob/main/examples/avenor-mcp/settings.yaml) loads `examples/avenor-mcp`, selects `mcp_servers: [avenor]` on a profile, and disables ambient `mcp`, `feeds`, and `cli_registry` defaults so the MCP inbox does not contend with the older CLI+feed example in `examples/avenor/`.

```sh
poo run --settings examples/avenor-mcp/settings.yaml \
  "spawn a child to run the test suite, then answer its questions"
```

- [CLI Registry & Script Tools](/capabilities/cli-registry) — wrap local CLIs and scripts without an MCP server
- [Feeds & Daemon](/capabilities/feeds-and-daemon) — command feeds, filters, and idle wake behavior
- [Built-in Tools & Jobs](/capabilities/tools-and-jobs) — `jobs`, `cancel_job`, and background execution
- [Manifests Reference](/reference/manifests) — complete manifest reference

<!-- Source: capabilities/codemode.md -->

# Codemode

Codemode lets the model write a short script to orchestrate tool calls instead of issuing them one turn at a time. Intermediate tool outputs stay inside the script, and only what the script prints and returns enters the conversation context.

In `poo`, codemode is not a privileged escape hatch: it is wired through `poo`'s nested-call seam (`poo.NestedCaller`). Every tool call a script makes passes through the same permission engine, doom-loop detector, and session log as a direct call from the model.

## How it works

1. The model invokes the `codemode` tool with a `script` argument.
2. `poo` runs the script inside a sandboxed engine (`poo/codemode.Engine`) that exposes no host filesystem, network, or timers — only the session's offered tools.
3. Each tool call the script makes is dispatched through `poo.NestedCaller`:
   - **Permissions:** Every nested call is judged individually by the [permission policy and asker chain](/operations/permissions-and-safety). A refusal or error is returned to the script as structured data (`outcome`, `is_error`) rather than crashing the run.
   - **Doom-loop detection:** Repeated identical or near-identical calls inside a script count toward the session's doom-loop thresholds.
   - **Session logging:** Each nested call is recorded in the [session log](/reference/session-log-v0) with mode `"nested"` and the parent `codemode` call's handle.
   - **Single-level nesting:** A script cannot invoke `codemode` itself.
4. Nested tool calls keep up to 1,000,000 characters of output internally so the script can filter or summarize large results. Only the script's printed lines and final return value are sent back to the model, bounded by `output_cap_chars` and the session's observation cap.
5. If a script fails or times out partway through, `poo` still reports the call count and prior printed output. The model can then see what already ran.

## Engines

`poo` ships two engines behind the `poo/codemode.Engine` interface. A custom binary that links no engine offers no `codemode` tool; see [Build Your Own Binary](/extending/custom-binary) for wiring engines.

### QuickJS (default)

`poo/codemode/quickjs` runs QuickJS-NG compiled to WebAssembly under `wazero`. It requires no Node.js installation, mounts an inert null filesystem, and provides no network or timer APIs.

A script is the body of an async JavaScript function:

```js
const files = await Promise.all([
  tools.read({ path: "README.md" }),
  tools.read({ path: "go.mod" }),
]);
return files.map((r) => (r.is_error ? r.text : r.text.split("\n")[0]));
```

Key primitives:

- `await tools.<name>(args)` invokes a session tool and resolves to `{ handle, tool, outcome, text, is_error, structured }`. `structured` is a native JSON value (or `null` when absent; invalid JSON remains a string).
- `Promise.all([...])` batches calls together. A batch executes concurrently when every call in it is read-only; otherwise calls run in submission order.
- `await parallel(() => [...])` overlaps independent calls, including writes. Tool promises must be created synchronously inside the callback and returned once each:

  ```js
  const [a, b] = await parallel(() => [
    tools.edit({ path: "a.txt", old: "draft", new: "final" }),
    tools.edit({ path: "b.txt", old: "draft", new: "final" }),
  ]);
  ```

  If two `poo` writes overlap on the same resolved path in one process, one returns `is_error: true` with `structured: { code: "edit_conflict" }`. `poo` does not detect shell command conflicts or roll back a batch.
- `print(value)` appends a line to the script's output; `return value` returns a JSON value.
- Batches run in submission order, with at most 16 calls per batch.

### Starlark

`poo/codemode/starlark` runs scripts in Starlark, a deterministic Python-like dialect with no file, network, clock, module-loading, or recursion capabilities, and an explicit execution-step budget (`exec_steps`).

Enable it with `tools.codemode.engine: starlark`:

```yaml
tools:
  codemode:
    engine: starlark
    exec_steps: 250000
```

Starlark builtins:

- `call(name, args)` runs one tool call and returns a dict with `handle`, `tool`, `outcome`, `text`, `is_error`, and `structured`.
- `gather([(name, args), ...])` runs a batch of up to 16 calls in list order (concurrently when all calls are read-only, sequentially otherwise).
- `json.decode(text)` and `json.encode(value)` convert between JSON strings and Starlark values.
- `print(x)` records an output line.
- `exit(value)` ends the script and returns `value` as JSON.

## Background execution

`codemode` supports background execution like other [background-capable tools](/capabilities/tools-and-jobs). Pass `background: true` on the tool call to run the script as a background job:

- The script's nested tool calls continue running after the originating turn ends, up to the job's timeout (`jobs.timeout_s`).
- Its output and return value arrive as a job result when the script finishes.
- Nested calls inside a batch cannot themselves request background jobs.

## Configuration

Configure codemode under `tools.codemode` in your settings file (see [Settings Reference](/reference/settings)):

```yaml
tools:
  codemode:
    engine: quickjs          # or "starlark"
    timeout_s: 120           # seconds per run
    script_max_bytes: 65536
    output_cap_chars: 16384
```

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tools.codemode.engine` | string | `"quickjs"` | Script runtime: `"quickjs"` or `"starlark"`. |
| `tools.codemode.timeout_s` | int | `120` | Wall-clock limit for one script run, in seconds. |
| `tools.codemode.script_max_bytes` | int | `65536` | Maximum accepted script length in bytes (64 KiB). |
| `tools.codemode.output_cap_chars` | int | `16384` | Maximum printed characters retained before truncation (16 KiB). |
| `tools.codemode.exec_steps` | int | `10000000` (Starlark) | Execution step budget. Supported by Starlark only; setting it with QuickJS (or an unset engine) is a configuration error. |

To disable codemode in a session or profile, add `codemode` to `tools.disabled` or `profiles.<name>.tools.disabled`.
