<!-- Source: operations/permissions-and-safety.md -->

# Permissions & Safety

Every tool call passes through the permission policy (`poo/perm`) before it executes. The policy runs as the first before-tool hook and resolves each call to either **allow** or **deny**. Calls configured to **ask** block on the asker chain until an asker answers or the chain falls back.

## Evaluation Order

The policy evaluates each tool call in a fixed order:

1. **Doom-loop detection** — checks exact and near repeat counts first, including for malformed calls that failed argument preparation.
2. **Policy rules** — checks `permission.rules` in order; the first matching rule wins.
3. **Outside-working-dir asks** — if the tool sets `ask_outside_working_dir: true` and the target path resolves outside the working directory, routes the call to `ask` (bypassing both read-only auto-allow and `permission.unmatched`).
4. **Read-only auto-allow** — any remaining unmatched `read_only` tool call is allowed.
5. **Unmatched action** — any remaining unmatched `side_effecting` tool call takes `permission.unmatched`.

## Permission Rules

Rules live under `permission.rules` and are evaluated top to bottom. Each rule must specify `action` (`allow`, `ask`, or `deny`) and match either a `tool` name or a `class` (`read_only` or `side_effecting`), never both.

```yaml
permission:
  unmatched: ask
  fallback: deny
  rules:
    - tool: bash
      command_contains: ["rm -rf", "sudo", "curl | sh"]
      action: ask
    - tool: bash
      command_prefix: "git status"
      action: allow
    - tool: fetch
      command_prefix: "docs.example.com"
      action: allow
    - tool: fetch
      command_prefix: "https://api.example.com/v1/"
      action: allow
    - class: read_only
      action: allow
```

### Rule Fields

| Field | Applies to | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `tool` | Exact tool name | Matches a single tool (e.g., `bash`, `edit`, `fetch`). Mutually exclusive with `class`. |
| `class` | Tool class | Matches `read_only` or `side_effecting` tools. Mutually exclusive with `tool`. |
| `command_prefix` | Named `tool` only | Matches the prefix of the tool's primary argument (`command` for `bash`, `url` for `fetch`). Mutually exclusive with `command_contains`. |
| `command_contains` | Named `tool` only | List of non-empty substrings; matches if any substring appears anywhere in the tool's primary argument. Mutually exclusive with `command_prefix`. |
| `action` | Required | `allow`, `ask`, or `deny`. |

### Prefix Matching and URL Hostname Rules

For non-URL arguments such as `bash` commands, `command_prefix` trims leading whitespace and performs a plain lexical prefix check. Because compound shell commands match their leading segment (`git status && rm -rf x` matches `git status`), `command_prefix` is a heuristic rather than a security boundary.

For tools whose primary argument is an absolute `http` or `https` URL (such as `fetch`), `command_prefix` uses canonical URL matching:

- **With a scheme** (`https://api.example.com/v1/`): matches only that scheme, host (or its subdomains), and path prefix.
- **Without a scheme** (`docs.example.com`): acts as a **hostname rule**. The call's own scheme decides, so a single rule covers both `http` and `https` URLs for that host and its subdomains.
- Query strings and fragments are ignored during comparison. Adjacent hosts (such as `evil-docs.example.com`) do not match.

### Substring Matching (`command_contains`)

`command_contains` matches when any listed substring appears anywhere in the tool's primary argument after trimming leading whitespace.

::: warning Tripwire, not a safety boundary
`command_contains` is plain text matching. A command spelled around a substring — using extra spaces, split flags, quoting, or shell variables — will not match. Use `command_contains` as a tripwire to prompt on risky patterns, and pair it with a [bubblewrap sandbox](/operations/sandbox) when hard isolation is required.
:::

## Unmatched Calls and Fallback

| Setting | CLI Flag | Default | Valid Values | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `permission.unmatched` | `--permission-unmatched` | `ask` | `allow`, `ask`, `deny` | Action for a `side_effecting` call that no rule matches. |
| `permission.fallback` | `--permission-fallback` | `deny` | `allow`, `deny` | Decision when the asker chain is exhausted, times out, or has no available asker. |

A policy can produce an `ask` via `unmatched: ask`, an `ask` rule, `ask_outside_working_dir`, or an explicit doom-loop `ask`. If no configured asker can ever answer in the current mode, poo emits a load-time warning naming the `fallback` decision.

## Asker Chain

When a call resolves to `ask`, the policy queries the askers listed in `permission.askers` in order. Each asker can return `allow`, `deny`, or `defer` (errors, panics, timeouts, and unavailable askers all defer to the next link). The entire chain is bounded by `permission.chain_timeout_s` (default `120` seconds).

Setting `permission.askers: []` explicitly configures an empty chain, sending every ask straight to `permission.fallback`. Omitting `askers` uses the binary's default chain.

```yaml
permission:
  askers: [decide, wire]
  chain_timeout_s: 120
  fallback: deny
  decide:
    allow: 0.85
    deny: 0.99
    timeout_ms: 1500
```

### Built-in Askers

- **`decide`** — queries the configured decision model (`roles.decide`) with recent conversation turns, the working directory, and the tool call arguments. If the model's `yes` probability meets `permission.decide.allow` (default `0.85`), the call is allowed; if `no` meets `permission.decide.deny` (default `0.99`), it is denied. Any lower confidence, error, or timeout (`permission.decide.timeout_ms`, default `1500` ms) defers to the next asker. Skipped automatically if no decision model is configured.
- **`wire`** — sends a `permission/ask` request to a connected `poo serve` client (such as `poo repl`) that declared the `permission_answers` capability. Default per-asker budget is `60` seconds (capped by the remaining chain timeout). Defers if no capable client is connected.

## Doom-Loop Detection

The core tracks consecutive repeats of tool calls and hands the counts to the permission policy before rules are checked:

```yaml
permission:
  doom_loop:
    threshold: 3
    near_threshold: 5
    action: ask
```

| Field | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `threshold` | `3` | Exact repeat count (same tool and arguments) that triggers the doom-loop action. |
| `near_threshold` | `5` | Near repeat count (same call shape) that triggers the doom-loop action. |
| `action` | `ask` | Action taken when either threshold is reached: `allow`, `ask`, or `deny`. |

When `action` is `allow` (or an asker allows the call), the repeat counter resets. When denied, the model receives a refusal message stating how many times the call was repeated so it can change approach.

## Protected Paths

`tools.protected_paths` lists path globs that file tools refuse to read, search, edit, or write:

```yaml
tools:
  protected_paths:
    - "**/.env"
    - "**/.env.*"
    - "~/.ssh/**"
```

Protected paths apply regardless of `restrict_to_working_dir` or `ask_outside_working_dir`. Under the `local` bash executor, `tools.protected_paths` only guards the built-in file tools — `bash` commands can still read any path the host process can. Under the `bwrap` executor, protected paths inside bound directories are masked with empty mounts. See [Sandboxing (bwrap)](/operations/sandbox) for details.

## Working Directory Boundaries

By default, file tools (`read`, `grep`, `edit`, `write`) can access paths outside the session's working directory. You can confine them or require approval per tool:

### Restrict to Working Directory

```yaml
tools:
  read:  { restrict_to_working_dir: true }
  grep:  { restrict_to_working_dir: true }
  edit:  { restrict_to_working_dir: true }
  write: { restrict_to_working_dir: true }
```

`restrict_to_working_dir: true` rejects paths outside the working directory before the permission policy runs. Restricted `read` is still permitted to read the session's configured skill directories.

### Ask Outside Working Directory

```yaml
tools:
  read:  { ask_outside_working_dir: true }
  grep:  { ask_outside_working_dir: true }
  edit:  { ask_outside_working_dir: true }
  write: { ask_outside_working_dir: true }
```

`ask_outside_working_dir: true` keeps outside paths reachable, but routes calls whose resolved path lies outside the working directory through the asker chain. This runs after `permission.rules` are evaluated and overrides both `permission.unmatched` and the `read_only` auto-allow.

If both `restrict_to_working_dir` and `ask_outside_working_dir` are enabled on the same tool, the restriction runs first. Only paths the restriction still permits outside the working directory (such as skill directories on `read`) reach the ask.

::: tip File tool limits do not confine `bash`
Neither `restrict_to_working_dir` nor `ask_outside_working_dir` restricts `bash` commands. For process and filesystem isolation, run commands through the [bubblewrap sandbox](/operations/sandbox).
:::

## Child Environment Filtering

`tools.env` controls which environment variables child processes (such as `bash` commands) inherit from the session:

```yaml
tools:
  env:
    scrub:
      - OPENAI_API_KEY
      - ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
      - AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
```

- **`tools.env.scrub`** — removes the listed variable names from the child environment while passing through everything else.
- **`tools.env.passthrough`** — restricts the child environment to *only* the listed variable names, dropping all others.

Separately, a launcher can set `POO_CREDENTIAL_ENV` (colon-separated variable names on Unix) to keep credential variables available to manifests via `env:NAME` bindings while withholding them from `bash` commands. See [Sandboxing (bwrap)](/operations/sandbox) for launcher credential details.

---

<!-- Source: operations/sandbox.md -->

# The sandbox

Poo runs the commands a model asks for through an **executor**. The
executor decides where the command runs. There are two:

| Executor | Package | What it contains |
|---|---|---|
| `local` (default) | `poo/tool/bash` | nothing: the command runs in poo's own process space, and it can reach anything poo can |
| `bwrap` | `poo/exec/bwrap` | a bubblewrap sandbox: a namespace of its own, with a filesystem of its own |

The `bwrap` executor is Linux-only, and it is opt-in: a binary links the
executors it wants, and a session picks one by name. A name the binary
does not link is a configuration error, and so is a `bwrap` that cannot
start. Neither falls back to the local executor.

## What the `bwrap` executor contains

The command runs in a bubblewrap sandbox with:

- **Every namespace it can have.** The command does not see the host's
  processes, its cgroups or its host name.
- **A fresh `/proc`, `/dev` and `/tmp`.** The command sees its own
  processes and nobody else's.
- **The system directories, read-only:** `/usr`, `/bin`, `/lib`,
  `/lib64` and `/etc` by default. The settings may name a different
  list.
- **The working directory, read-write.** It is the only place the
  command can write, beside the extra read-write binds the settings
  name.
- **The network**, unless the settings cut it
  (`tools.bwrap.network: false`). The network is the host's, and with
  it the resolver's directory (`/run/systemd/resolve`) is mounted
  read-only, because `/etc/resolv.conf` is often a link into it.
- **The fetch tool is not a command**, and the sandbox does not see
  it: the fetch runs in poo's own process, over the host's network,
  whatever `tools.bwrap.network` says. What bounds it is the tool's
  own guard: loopback and private addresses are refused unless
  `tools.fetch.allow_private_hosts` says otherwise, and link-local and
  the reserved ranges are refused whatever the settings say. A session
  that must not reach the network disables the tool
  (`tools.disabled: [fetch]`).

`$HOME` is not mounted. The operator's files are not the command's,
unless a bind names them.

### Protected paths

A protected path inside a bound directory is masked: a directory behind
an empty tmpfs, a file behind an empty device. The executor asks the
matcher about every bind, so this covers the working directory, the
read-only system directories and the extra read-write binds alike. The
command reads nothing where the configuration protects something. A
protected path outside every bound directory is not in the sandbox at
all. A protected path that is a link is masked where the link points,
because a mount cannot land on a link. The expansion of a bind is reused
by the commands that follow, so a large read-only bind is walked once,
not once per command.

The `local` executor cannot do this. Protected paths stop the file
tools from wandering; with the `local` executor, `bash` reaches
everything the process can.

The paths are the settings' `tools.protected_paths`, and
`examples/code.settings.yaml` shows the setting with a commented
example: the operator's own secrets, protected from a model that goes
looking.

### What ends the sandbox

The sandbox ends when the command ends, and the kernel ends a
namespace when its init dies. A descendant that leaves the process
group (`setsid`, a double fork into a new session) therefore dies with
the call, which is the escape the `local` executor cannot close.

A background job runs in a sandbox of its own, and `cancel_job` or
`session/close` stops it the same way.

The sandbox ends with poo as well. The helper that runs the command is
the sandbox's init, and it holds one end of a pipe whose other end poo
holds: the kernel closes it when poo ends, and the helper takes the
command down and exits, which ends the namespace. The executor also
starts bubblewrap with `--die-with-parent` and the parent-death signal,
so the bubblewrap process does not outlive poo either. A poo that is
killed without a teardown therefore leaves no sandbox behind. The
`local` executor has no such tie, so a command it runs outlives a killed
poo.

## Launcher credentials

A launcher can set `POO_CREDENTIAL_ENV` to the names of credentials poo's
feeds or registered tools need. Separate names with the operating system's
path-list separator (`:` on Linux and macOS). The variable lists names,
not their values; the launcher supplies the values separately.

The session environment keeps these values, so a feed or a registered tool
can receive one through an explicit manifest `env:NAME` binding. A `bash`
command does not inherit the declared names in its environment. A registered
tool that receives a credential can still use or disclose it, so trust its
manifest and command.

This differs from `tools.env.scrub`, which removes names from the session
environment too. A feed or tool binding cannot resolve a name removed there
or excluded by `tools.env.passthrough`. Environment scrubbing is not process
isolation: with the `local` executor, a command can read poo's environment
through procfs as described below.

## Registered tools

A registered tool — whether the session offers it directly or runs it
through `call_cli` — runs where a bash command runs: through the session's
executor, with the sandbox's binds and the protected paths it masks.

- **The command is the one its manifest names**, and the executor wraps
  it the way it wraps a shell command. A `bwrap` session runs it in the
  sandbox, and a protected path is masked there.
- **Its directory** is the manifest's when the manifest fixes one, and
  the session's working directory otherwise.
- **Its environment** is the session's environment, already scrubbed: the
  benign names the tool needs (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LANG`, `LC_ALL`, `TMPDIR`)
  come from it, then the variables the manifest declares, with an
  `env:NAME` reference resolved against the scrubbed environment, and a
  `session:id` reference resolved to the session's own ID at the call.
  A name the scrub removed, or a `tools.env.passthrough` list left out, is a
  reference the call cannot honour, and it fails naming the variable.
  A manifest can explicitly pass a credential declared through
  `POO_CREDENTIAL_ENV` using an `env:NAME` binding.
- **Its arguments** were checked against the manifest's schema before the
  process started, so a malformed call never runs. The same check, in the
  library, refuses a value that begins with a dash when the manifest
  passes it as an argument of its own (`style: space`), because a command
  whose flag takes no value would read it as another flag. The rule
  belongs to `cli-registry` (`specs/argv.md` there): the call fails its
  validation, naming the property, before argv exists. Bind the property
  `equals` to pass a value that looks like one — a dash-leading value
  inside one `--flag=value` element is not an option, even when it spells
  one the manifest fixes itself.
- **Its lifetime** is the plan's timeout, enforced by poo, and the run's
  context: a timeout, an interrupt, a cancel, a close or
  `--no-wait-jobs` stops the tool and everything it started in its process
  group.
- **The output is bash's envelope**: both streams, the exit status, null
  for a killed process, and the partial output of a timeout.

The `local` executor still cannot hide what it does not own: a tool it
runs can read poo's own environment through `/proc/$PPID/environ`,
because the process that started it is poo. The `bwrap` executor closes
that, because the tool's parent is inside the sandbox's pid namespace.
Scrubbing stops a manifest reference; only isolation stops procfs.

## What the `bwrap` executor does not contain

**It is not a security boundary against hostile code.**

- **The kernel is the host's.** The sandbox is a namespace, not a
  kernel: a kernel bug is reachable from inside it.
- **The network is the host's**, unless it is cut. With the network on,
  the command can reach anything the host can reach, and the host can
  reach the command's ports.
- **The user is the host's user**, in a user namespace. The files the
  user owns are readable whenever they are bound.
- **A bind is a hole.** A read-write bind hands the command the
  directory it names, whatever is in it.

The sandbox is for keeping a model's commands inside the task: the
working directory, the fixtures, and nothing else. It is not for
running code you do not trust.

## Running all of poo inside a sandbox

The executor keeps the model's commands apart from poo. When the whole
process has to be contained -- a run on a shared machine, a run that
must not see the operator's files at all -- run poo itself inside
bubblewrap or a container. That is the portable option, and the only
one on macOS, where namespaces are not available to an unprivileged
process.

A whole-process sandbox for a poo run:

```sh
bwrap \
  --unshare-all --share-net --die-with-parent --new-session \
  --ro-bind /usr /usr --symlink usr/bin /bin --symlink usr/sbin /sbin \
  --symlink usr/lib /lib --symlink usr/lib64 /lib64 \
  --ro-bind /etc /etc \
  --ro-bind-try /run/systemd/resolve /run/systemd/resolve \
  --proc /proc --dev /dev --tmpfs /tmp \
  --bind "$PWD" /work \
  --chdir /work \
  --setenv HOME /tmp \
  -- poo run --working-dir /work --log /work/session.jsonl "..."
```

The container is the same idea with a different tool:

```sh
docker run --rm -it --network none -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work ghcr.io/sdougbrown/poo \
  poo run --working-dir /work --log /work/session.jsonl "..."
```

The eval harness does the first of these: `poo-eval run --isolation bwrap`
wraps the whole `poo` process, and `poo-eval run --executor bwrap`
wraps the model's commands in a sandbox of their own, bound to the
task's workdir. The two are layers, not alternatives: a run may use
both, and each closes what the other leaves open.

---

<!-- Source: operations/sessions-and-durability.md -->

# Sessions & Durability

Poo persists session transcripts, tool outcomes, permission decisions, and run state as append-only records. For the exact on-disk record schemas, see [Session Log v0](/reference/session-log-v0).

## Persistence Modes

Configure persistence with `session.mode` (or `--ephemeral` on the CLI):

| Mode | Persistence | Crash Behavior on Reload |
|---|---|---|
| `logged` (default) | Writes one JSONL file per session under `session.dir` (`~/.local/state/poo/sessions` by default). | Truncates torn tails; settles unfinished runs, in-flight tool calls, and jobs as `interrupted`. |
| `ephemeral` | Keeps records in memory for the lifetime of the process. Writes nothing to disk. | Cannot be loaded or resumed. |
| `durable` | Persists records (JSONL or SQLite) under `session.dir` with lease-based ownership. | Truncates torn tails and builds a continuation plan to resume the unsettled run instead of settling it interrupted. |

```yaml
session:
  mode: durable
  dir: ~/.local/state/poo/sessions
  durable:
    store: sqlite
    lease_ttl_s: 30
    max_resumptions: 3
    auto_resume: false
```

## Storage Backends: JSONL vs. SQLite

Logged sessions always use the file-backed JSONL store. Durable sessions select a backend via `session.durable.store`:

| Backend | Setting Value | Files on Disk | Locking / Ownership |
|---|---|---|---|
| **File (JSONL)** | `file` (default) | `<dir>/<session_id>.jsonl`, `<dir>/<session_id>.lock` (and `<dir>/<session_id>.lease` when leased) | `flock` for `logged`; lease file + short critical-section `flock` for `durable`. |
| **SQLite** | `sqlite` | `<dir>/sessions.db` (WAL journaling) | Row-based leases in the `leases` table; every write and lease transition runs in an immediate transaction. |

SQLite stores session metadata in `sessions`, append-only records in `records`, and ownership leases in `leases` with indexed queries.

## Locking and Lease TTLs

Poo enforces single-writer exclusivity on every open session:

- **File lock (`flock`)** — Used by `logged` sessions. Opening a session acquires an exclusive non-blocking `flock` on `<session_id>.lock` and holds it until the store closes. If the process crashes, the OS kernel releases the lock immediately so another process can recover the session.
- **Lease authority (`lease_ttl_s`)** — Used by `durable` sessions (and all SQLite-backed sessions). Opening a session acquires a lease with a unique 16-byte fencing token and a TTL configured by `session.durable.lease_ttl_s` (default `30` seconds). A background heartbeat renews the lease every `TTL / 3` seconds.
  - While the lease is live, another process attempting to open the session is refused with `ErrSessionLocked`.
  - If the owner dies or stops heartbeating past `expires_at`, a new owner can take over the lease. The takeover logs a warning naming the previous owner and expiry time.
  - Once a lease is lost or taken over, the previous owner is fenced by its token. Subsequent writes fail with `ErrLeaseLost`, and late releases leave the new owner's lease untouched.

## Crash Recovery and Resumption

Loading a stored session (`session/load` over the wire, `session.Resume` in Go, or `poo repl --continue` / `--resume`) scans the session log and recovers any incomplete state.

### Logged Recovery

1. Any torn trailing JSONL line from a mid-write crash is truncated.
2. Unsettled runs are marked `interrupted`.
3. In-flight tool calls and background jobs without results receive an `interrupted` outcome (`outcome unknown; the process stopped during this call` / `...this job`) so the model knows the effect is uncertain.
4. Undelivered job results are re-queued for the session.

### Durable Recovery (`auto_resume` and `max_resumptions`)

Instead of settling the latest unfinished run as interrupted, `durable` mode runs the `DurablePlanner` to build a continuation plan:

- **Tool calls** — `read_only` calls, `idempotent` tools, and side-effecting calls whose start record never landed are scheduled for replay. Side-effecting calls that already started are settled as `interrupted` so the model can decide how to proceed.
- **Permission asks** — Asks whose wall-clock deadline has not passed remain live and are re-armed; expired asks are resolved using their recorded `fallback` decision.
- **Partial output & compaction** — Partial assistant messages and uncommitted compactions are discarded cleanly; the run resumes at the appropriate phase (`requesting`, `streaming`, `executing`, or `waiting`).
- **Session jobs & feeds** — Running jobs and in-flight feed attempts died with the previous process and are ended as `interrupted`; feed subscriptions are restored.

Two settings control resumption behavior:

- **`session.durable.max_resumptions`** (default `3`) — Maximum number of times a single run may be resumed across crashes. Once reached, the planner stops continuing the run and settles it as `interrupted` with `resumption_limit` to prevent infinite crash loops.
- **`session.durable.auto_resume`** (default `false`) — When `false`, a loaded durable session holds its continuation plan idle until explicitly resumed. When `true`, loading the session automatically resumes the unsettled run.

## Explicit Log Path (`--log`)

On `poo run`, `--log <path>` writes the session log to a specific file path instead of `session.dir`.

```bash
poo run --log ./traces/build-fix.jsonl "Fix the failing unit tests"
```

`--log` always creates a new file and refuses to extend or overwrite an existing file.

## Managing Sessions

### Listing Sessions

`poo sessions list` inspects the configured session directory (override with `--session-dir`):

```bash
poo sessions list
poo sessions list --json
```

Table columns: `ID`, `CREATED`, `PROFILE`, `RUNS`, `REASON`, `SIZE`, and `LOCKED`.

### Pruning and Retention

Retention is opt-in — without a configured policy or CLI flags, `poo sessions prune` deletes nothing and exits with a usage error.

Configure defaults in settings under `session.retention`:

```yaml
session:
  retention:
    max_age_days: 30
    max_sessions: 200
```

Run `poo sessions prune` to apply the configured policy or override it with flags:

```bash
# Preview what would be deleted
poo sessions prune --dry-run

# Delete sessions with no activity in the last 14 days, keeping at most 50
poo sessions prune --older-than 14 --keep 50
```

| Setting | CLI Flag | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `session.retention.max_age_days` | `--older-than <days>` | Delete sessions whose last activity is older than this many days. |
| `session.retention.max_sessions` | `--keep <count>` | Keep at most this many most recently active sessions. |
| — | `--dry-run` | Print sessions that would be deleted without removing them. |

Sessions currently held by another process (`LOCKED: true`) are always skipped during pruning.

---

<!-- Source: operations/limits-and-exit-codes.md -->

# Limits & Exit Codes

`poo` enforces explicit per-run limits and maps every run outcome to a distinct process exit code. Scripts, CI jobs, and supervisors can distinguish natural completion from budgets, provider failures, and configuration errors.

## Run Limits

Configure run limits under `limits` in your settings file (see [Settings Reference](/reference/settings)). Every limit must be non-negative (`>= 0`). Setting a budget to `0` disables it, except `max_continuations`, where `0` selects the default (`3`).

| Setting | Type | Default | CLI Flag (`poo run`) | Settle Reason (Exit Code) | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `limits.max_tokens_per_run` | int | `0` (off) | — | `budget_exhausted` (`14`) | Total token budget for a single run (settle source `max_run_tokens`). |
| `limits.max_duration_s` | int (seconds) | `0` (off) | — (see `--timeout` below) | `budget_exhausted` (`14`) | Wall-clock duration budget for a run, evaluated between turns (settle source `max_duration`). |
| `limits.max_turns` | int | `0` (off) | `--max-turns` | `max_turns` (`11`) | Maximum number of model turns per run. |
| `limits.max_continuations` | int | `3` | — | `hook_continue_limit` (`12`) | Maximum `BeforeSettle` hook continuations allowed in one run. |
| `limits.truncation_retries` | int | `1` | `--truncation-retries` | `output_truncated` (`10`) | Consecutive output-limit truncations the run asks the model to retry more concisely before settling. Set to `0` to settle on the first truncation. |

```yaml
version: 1
limits:
  max_tokens_per_run: 500000
  max_duration_s: 300
  max_turns: 25
  max_continuations: 3
  truncation_retries: 1
```

### `limits.max_duration_s` vs. `poo run --timeout`

These two controls are distinct:

- **`limits.max_duration_s`** is a run budget. The session checks elapsed time at turn boundaries and settles cleanly with `budget_exhausted` (exit code `14`, detail source `max_duration`).
- **`poo run --timeout <duration>`** sets a Go context deadline on the invocation. When the deadline expires, the in-flight request or tool call is cancelled immediately and the run settles with `cancelled` (exit code `130`, detail source `cancel:deadline`).

## Settle-Reason Exit Codes (`poo run`)

Every settled run records a closed, typed `Reason` (defined in `reason.go`). `poo run` exits with the code for that reason:

| Exit Code | Settle Reason(s) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `0` | `end_turn`, `finished`, `stop_requested` | Run completed normally: the model stopped on its own (`end_turn`), called the `finish` tool with a valid result (`finished`), or stopped at a hook/stop condition's request (`stop_requested`). |
| `1` | *(unclassified / operational)* | Operational failure with no settle-reason code of its own (for example, transport setup failure, session start failure, or an unknown settle reason). |
| `2` | *(usage / configuration)* | Command refused its arguments, settings, working directory, or a system prompt that failed to render. |
| `10` | `output_truncated` | Provider stopped at the output-token limit and all `truncation_retries` were spent. |
| `11` | `max_turns` | Run reached `limits.max_turns` / `--max-turns`. |
| `12` | `hook_continue_limit` | `BeforeSettle` hooks requested more continuations than `limits.max_continuations`. |
| `13` | `context_exhausted` | Context window filled and could not be compacted further. |
| `14` | `budget_exhausted` | Run exhausted `limits.max_tokens_per_run` or `limits.max_duration_s`. |
| `15` | `invalid_turns` | Model produced unusable turns (for example, unparseable or missing tool calls) for the maximum consecutive turns allowed. |
| `20` | `provider_error` | Provider request failed and could not be retried, or the retry budget was spent. |
| `21` | `tool_fatal` | A tool returned a fatal error (`ErrFatal`), indicating an unusable environment. |
| `22` | `hook_error` | An executable hook failed or missed its deadline. |
| `23` | `store_error` | Session store failed; the session is marked broken. |
| `24` | `provider_limit` | Provider refused the request for quota or plan reasons (the session itself is not broken). |
| `130` | `cancelled` | Run was cancelled by `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM` or `--timeout`. |

::: tip Signal handling in `poo run`
The first `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM` cancels the active run so it can settle cleanly and exit `130`. A second interrupt forces immediate session teardown (bounded to 250 ms) and exits `130`.
:::

### Precedence and Multi-Run Exit Codes

- **Arbitration order:** When multiple settle candidates occur on the same turn, higher-severity reasons win. `cancelled` beats all other reasons, followed by failures (`store_error`, `hook_error`, `tool_fatal`, `provider_limit`/`provider_error`), then limits (`context_exhausted`, `hook_continue_limit`, `max_turns`, `budget_exhausted`, `invalid_turns`), and finally natural stops (`finished`, `stop_requested`, `output_truncated`, `end_turn`).
- **Background job wakes:** When `poo run` waits for background jobs (unless `--no-wait-jobs` is set), job completions can wake follow-up runs within the same session. `poo run` combines exit codes across all settled runs so the **first non-zero exit code wins**; exit `0` requires every settled run to succeed.

## `poo daemon` Exit Codes

`poo daemon` hosts a long-lived durable session driven by feeds (see [Feeds & Daemon](/capabilities/feeds-and-daemon) and [CLI Reference](/reference/cli#poo-daemon)). Its exit codes report daemon lifecycle status to a process supervisor:

| Exit Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | Clean shutdown after `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM` (feeds stopped, records flushed, lease released). |
| `1` | Operational failure or **lost lease**. Happens if another process takes the lease, the store fails to open or resume, or resuming a pending run breaks the session. |
| `2` | Usage, argument, settings, or invalid `--session` ID error. |

---

<!-- Source: extending/architecture.md -->

# Architecture

Poo is a modular Go agent harness designed as a library first. The core package owns the agent loop, tool registry, hook points, event stream, and session lifecycle. Everything else—tools, executors, providers, persistence stores, and the wire server—is an opt-in package wired at compile time. What a binary does not link cannot be reached at runtime.

## Package layout

Packages are grouped by subsystem:

### Core and contracts

| Package | Role |
|---|---|
| `poo` | Core agent loop FSM, tool registry, hooks, event stream, and session lifecycle |
| `poo/prompt` | System prompt vocabulary: named sections, variants, and template environment |
| `poo/decide` | Decision-model contract: questions, answers, `Decider`, and recording wrapper |
| `poo/exec` | Executor contract (`Executor`, `Command`, `Process`), registry, and env scrubbing |
| `poo/protect` | Protected-path matcher shared by tools and permission policy |
| `poo/pootest` | Exported test helpers: scripted transport, in-memory sink, stub decider, scripted compactor |

### Tools and execution

| Package | Role |
|---|---|
| `poo/tool/*` | Opt-in tools: `read`, `edit`, `write`, `grep`, `bash`, `cliregistry`, `callmcp`, `codemode`, `fetch`, `finish` |
| `poo/exec/bwrap` | Linux bubblewrap sandboxing executor |
| `poo/codemode/*` | Opt-in codemode engines (`quickjs`, `starlark`) |
| `poo/profile/*` | Named tool profiles (`code`, `search`, etc.) with default prompt and permission posture |

### Providers, permissions, and persistence

| Package | Role |
|---|---|
| `poo/provider/*` | Provider seam, model catalog (`provider/catalog`), and wire transports (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) |
| `poo/perm` | Permission engine: tool call policy, doom-loop detection, and asker chain |
| `poo/perm/decide` | Permission asker backed by a decision model |
| `poo/session` | Session persistence seam: store, versioned codec, history projection, and locking |
| `poo/session/sqlite` | Opt-in SQLite session store |

### Capabilities and integrations

| Package | Role |
|---|---|
| `poo/cli` | CLI registry catalog and manifest loader |
| `poo/feed` | Feed manifest loader, environment builder, and stdout record runner |
| `poo/mcp` | MCP client: server lifecycle, tool dispatch, resource feeds, and relaunch loop |
| `poo/mcp/manifest` | `mcp.json` manifest loader, launch templates, and resource feed declarations |
| `poo/skill` | Skill directory discovery and `SKILL.md` frontmatter loader |

### Server, wire, and CLI

| Package | Role |
|---|---|
| `poo/wire/protocol` | Public JSON-RPC 2.0 wire contract: method names, error codes, and request/result DTOs |
| `poo/wire` | JSON-RPC 2.0 server over stdio |
| `poo/wire/conformance` | Black-box protocol conformance suite and exported fake provider endpoint |
| `poo/server` | `wire.Factory` implementation bridging `config` and `wire` |
| `poo/config` | Opt-in settings loading, schema validation, and runtime assembly |
| `poo/cmd/poo` | Reference headless CLI and `poo serve` binary |

## Stdlib-only core rule

The core package (`poo`) depends only on the Go standard library plus `poo/prompt`, `poo/decide`, and `poo/scopeschema`—each of which imports only the standard library. Several contract packages are also strictly standard-library-only so clients and extensions can depend on them without pulling in the rest of the module:

- `poo/wire/protocol`
- `poo/prompt` and `poo/prompt/agentsmd`
- `poo/decide`
- `poo/exec`
- `poo/protect`
- `poo/caps`
- `poo/scopeschema`
- `poo/mcp/wire`

`internal/depcheck` enforces these boundaries during `go test`. It inspects each checked package's non-test dependency closure via `go list -e -deps -json`. The test suite fails if any package imports an unapproved internal or third-party dependency. For example, only `poo/mcp` may import the MCP Go SDK. A binary that omits an MCP launcher never links that SDK.

See [Build Your Own Binary](/extending/custom-binary#the-closure-gate) for how custom binaries enforce their own dependency exclusions.

## Session FSM

A session moves through a closed set of explicit states (`poo.State`). Consumers add behavior through hooks rather than introducing new states.

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `idle` | The session has no active run. |
| `requesting` | The run is requesting a response from the provider. |
| `streaming` | The provider's response stream is arriving. |
| `executing` | The run is executing tool calls requested by the model. |
| `compacting` | The run is compacting the conversation view before the next request. |
| `waiting` | The run is open while waiting on background jobs it started. |
| `settling` | The run is finalizing and recording its settle outcome. |
| `settled` | The run has completed; a new prompt transitions back to `requesting`. |

All state changes pass through a single transition function checked against the legal transition table (`poo.IsLegal`):

| From | Allowed next states |
|---|---|
| `idle` | `requesting` |
| `requesting` | `streaming`, `executing`, `compacting`, `requesting`, `waiting`, `settling` |
| `streaming` | `executing`, `requesting`, `compacting`, `waiting`, `settling` |
| `executing` | `executing`, `requesting`, `compacting`, `waiting`, `settling` |
| `compacting` | `requesting`, `waiting`, `settling` |
| `waiting` | `requesting`, `compacting`, `settling` |
| `settling` | `settled` |
| `settled` | `requesting` |

Once a run enters `settling` or `settled`, background work from the ending run cannot move it backwards; only a subsequent run moves `settled` back to `requesting`.

## Hook points

Hooks extend the session lifecycle without altering the FSM. Every hook receives a `poo.HookContext` carrying the session ID, run ID, turn number, read-only `HistoryView`, `ContextBudget`, and optional `Decider`. Hooks may append to history through their return decisions, never mutate prior messages in place. The context also carries `WorkingDir`, the directory the session's tools work in, and `ReadOnlyTools`, a bounded probe over the `read`, `grep` and `history` tools.

| Option / Interface | When it runs | Decisions / Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `WithSessionStart` (`SessionStartHook`) | Once when the session is built, before the first run | Append messages, edit system prompt sections (`StartDecision`) |
| `WithBeforeRun` (`BeforeRunHook`) | At the start of every run, before the first provider request | Append messages, edit system prompt sections (`StartDecision`) |
| `WithPolicy` (`PolicyHook`) | Before all other `BeforeTool` hooks; reserved for the permission engine | `Allow()` or `Deny(detail)` only; exempt from hook deadline |
| `WithBeforeTool` (`BeforeToolHook`) | After argument preparation and policy check, before tool execution | `Allow()`, `Deny(detail)`, or `ShortCircuit(ToolResult)` |
| `WithAfterTool` (`AfterToolHook`) | After a tool call finishes, before the model sees the result | `Keep()`, `Annotate(text)`, `Replace(ToolResult)`, or `Redact(ToolResult)` |
| `WithAfterTurn` (`AfterTurnHook`) | At the end of every turn, including interrupted turns | `AppendMessages(...)` or `StopTurn(detail)` |
| `WithBeforeSettle` (`BeforeSettleHook`) | When the model stops on its own | `Accept()`, `Continue(Message)`, or `StopSettle(detail)` |
| `WithStopCondition` (`StopCondition`) | At every turn end after the tool batch finishes | Ends the run when matched |
| `WithObserver` (`Observer`) | On every session event, in order | Read-only observation; never settles a run |
| `WithSessionAttach` (`AttachFunc`) | Once during live session construction (including resume), before feeds or runs | Attach session-owned subsystems (such as MCP servers) and return a close function |

Hooks that are safe to re-run after a crash mid-hook on durable sessions may implement `poo.IdempotentHook`. Hooks that do not implement it are never re-executed on recovery.

## Provider-neutral message model

The core maintains a single provider-neutral message representation for all supported wire APIs. It carries text, tool calls, tool results, reasoning or thinking blocks, opaque provider blocks, and image attachments. Transports translate this model to and from Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, and Anthropic Messages without leaking provider-specific types into the core.

For the exact round-trip mapping across all three APIs, see [Wire API Mapping](/reference/wire-api-mapping).

---

<!-- Source: extending/custom-binary.md -->

# Build Your Own Binary

Poo is a library first. A consumer composes only the packages it wants into its own binary—selecting the tools, executors, profiles, and providers it links. Anything the binary omits is not reachable at runtime because it is not compiled into the executable.

`cmd/poo` is one such composition. `wire/conformance/testdata/readonly` is the smallest: it serves the `search` profile, `read`, `grep`, and the OpenAI transport, with no shell and no tool capable of mutating state.

## Wiring `server.New` and `wire.Serve`

`server.New` takes loaded settings, linked tools, executors, and profiles, and returns a `*server.Server` that implements `wire.Factory`. Pass it to `wire.Serve` to expose the JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol over stdio:

```go
settings, err := config.Load(*settingsPath)
if err != nil {
	return err
}
srv, err := server.New(server.Options{
	Settings:       settings,
	WorkingDir:     dir,
	DefaultProfile: search.Name,
	Tools: map[string]config.ToolFactory{
		"read": func(config.ToolOptions) poo.Tool { return read.New() },
		"grep": func(config.ToolOptions) poo.Tool { return grep.New() },
	},
	Profiles: []profile.Profile{search.Profile()},
	Build:    poo.BuildInfo{Name: "poo-readonly", Version: version},
})
if err != nil {
	return err
}
return wire.Serve(wire.Options{
	In:      os.Stdin,
	Out:     os.Stdout,
	Factory: srv,
	Build: protocol.Build{
		Name:       "poo-readonly",
		Version:    version,
		PooVersion: version,
	},
})
```

### `wire.Factory`

`wire.Factory` is the seam between the wire transport (`poo/wire`) and your binary's runtime configuration. The wire server never reads settings or constructs sessions directly; it delegates to the factory:

- `Profiles()`, `DefaultProfile()`, `Capabilities()`, `Roles()`: reported during the `poo/initialize` handshake.
- `Create(...)` and `Load(...)`: construct or resume a `*poo.Session` for a client request, receiving a `wire.FactoryEnv` with the server's `Observer` and permission `Client`.
- `Configure(...)`: applies between-run session updates (model, reasoning, prompt variant, etc.).
- `Models(...)` and `Settings(...)`: serve `models/list` and `settings/get`.

`server.New` implements `wire.Factory` on top of `config.Build`, caching runtimes per profile/model combination while keeping each session's store, prompt overrides, and permission asks isolated.

## Profiles, executors, and session options

### Profiles and tools

`server.Options.Profiles` lists the profiles the binary offers, and `server.Options.Tools` maps tool names to `config.ToolFactory` constructors. Each map key must match the name returned by the tool's `Spec()`. A profile, permission rule, or manifest that references an unlinked tool fails validation with a typed error.

Use `server.Options.SessionTools` to mutate each runtime the factory builds before creating a session. For example, it can add `finish` for structured output when settings opt into a schema no profile lists.

### Executors

Register only the command executors your binary links using `exec.NewRegistry`:

```go
registry := exec.NewRegistry()
registry.Register("local", func(exec.Options) (exec.Executor, error) {
	return bash.NewLocal(), nil
})
```

Pass `registry` in `server.Options.Executors`. An executor is resolved only when a profile offers `bash` (or runs feeds or CLI registry commands). A read-only binary passes `nil` and cannot spawn commands. If settings request an executor name that is not registered, `config.Build` returns `exec.ErrUnknownExecutor` rather than falling back to another executor.

### Overrides and manifest paths

`server.Options.Overrides` carries CLI flag overrides (such as `FeedsPaths`, `CLIRegistryPaths`, and `MCPPaths`). `server.New` automatically merges environment overrides (`POO_FEEDS_PATH`, `POO_CLI_REGISTRY_PATH`, `POO_MCP_PATH`, `POO_SKILLS_PATH`) via `config.EnvOverrides`. A binary that calls `config.Build` directly must call `config.EnvOverrides` itself if it wants environment path support.

For manifest-driven capabilities that do not require linking custom Go tools, see:

- [CLI Registry & Script Tools](/capabilities/cli-registry)
- [Feeds & Daemon](/capabilities/feeds-and-daemon)
- [MCP Servers](/capabilities/mcp-servers)
- [Manifests Reference](/reference/manifests)

### Permission askers

`permission.askers` distinguishes between an absent list and an explicit empty list:

- **Absent**: uses the binary's default chain (`[wire]` in `server.New` / `poo serve`).
- **Explicit empty list (`[]`)**: configures a chain with no askers, so any `ask` decision goes straight to the configured fallback.

A chain may name an asker the runtime cannot provide, such as `wire` in headless `poo run`. That asker is dropped with a schema-backed warning (`fairWhen` on `has_wire_client`) instead of failing the settings file.

Over the wire, the `wire` asker only sends `permission/ask` requests to a client that declared `capabilities.permission_answers: true` in `poo/initialize`. Otherwise every ask falls back and `session/create` / `session/load` include a warning explaining the missing capability.

## Inspecting linked packages

Check which tool packages a binary actually links with `go list`:

```sh
go list -deps ./cmd/my-poo | grep 'poo/tool'
```

## The closure gate

The main security and footprint guarantee of composing your own binary is what it does *not* link. Enforce this in CI with a closure test that inspects `go list -deps`:

```go
deps := listDeps(t, "./wire/conformance/testdata/readonly")
for _, excluded := range []string{
	"tool/bash",
	"tool/edit",
	"tool/cliregistry",
	"tool/codemode",
	"tool/fetch",
	"codemode/starlark",
	"codemode/quickjs",
	"exec/bwrap",
	"mcp",
	"tool/callmcp",
} {
	if slices.Contains(deps, modulePath+"/"+excluded) {
		t.Errorf("the read-only binary links %s", excluded)
	}
}
```

`internal/depcheck/closure_test.go` implements this gate for the reference read-only binary. Always assert both **exclusions** (forbidden packages and third-party SDKs are absent) and **inclusions** (intended packages are present). Otherwise, a broken target that imports nothing could vacuously pass the exclusion check.

---

<!-- Source: extending/custom-tools-and-prompts.md -->

# Custom Tools & Prompts

When building a custom binary, you can inject Go tools directly into the runtime. You can also replace or extend embedded system prompt sections and supply custom command executors.

::: tip No-rebuild alternatives
To add tools without compiling Go, use [CLI Registry & Script Tools](/capabilities/cli-registry) or [MCP Servers](/capabilities/mcp-servers). The CLI registry also supports JSON stdin/stdout scripts in any language. See the [Manifests Reference](/reference/manifests) for schemas.
:::

## Injecting Go tools

### The `poo.Tool` interface

Every Go tool implements `poo.Tool`:

```go
type Tool interface {
	Spec() ToolSpec
	Prepare(raw json.RawMessage, env PrepareEnv) (Prepared, error)
	Call(ctx context.Context, in Prepared, env ToolEnv) (ToolResult, error)
}
```

- `Spec()` returns `poo.ToolSpec`: the tool's `Name`, `Description`, JSON `Schema`, side-effect `Class` (`ClassReadOnly` or `ClassSideEffecting`), optional `PrimaryArg` (used by doom-loop detection), `Background` mode (`BackgroundNever`, `BackgroundAllowed`, or `BackgroundAlways`), and `Idempotent` flag (whether a durable session may safely replay an interrupted call).
- `Prepare(raw, env)` decodes and validates raw JSON arguments with no side effects. Return `*poo.ErrInvalidArgs` (via `poo.InvalidArgsf`) for recoverable validation errors so the model can correct its call. The returned `poo.Prepared` provides `Summary() string` for transcripts and events.
- `Call(ctx, in, env)` executes the prepared call using `poo.ToolEnv` (working directory, scrubbed `Env`, `SessionID`, `RunID`, `Handle`, `JobID`, `Decider`, `History`, `Nested` caller, and `Settings`).

Optional interfaces a tool or its `Prepared` value may implement:

| Interface | Implemented by | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `poo.PromptContributor` | `Tool` | Contributes a `tools.<name>` system prompt section when the tool is linked and offered |
| `poo.PromptVariantContributor` | `Tool` | Provides variant-specific prompt text keyed by variant name |
| `poo.AskSummaryer` | `Prepared` | Supplies permission-ask text independent of model-authored summaries |
| `poo.CanonicalKeyer` | `Prepared` | Returns a canonical JSON key for doom-loop comparison |
| `poo.EvidenceArgumenter` | `Prepared` | Selects which arguments a decision model may inspect |
| `poo.BackgroundShorthander` | `Tool` | Translates shorthand syntax (such as trailing `&`) into a managed background job |
| `poo.BackgroundableCaller` | `Tool` | Reports that a running synchronous call can be moved into a background job |

### Registering with `config.ToolFactory`

Pass tool constructors in `server.Options.Tools` (or `config.BuildOptions.Tools`):

```go
type ToolFactory func(ToolOptions) poo.Tool

type ToolOptions struct {
	Executor       exec.Executor
	Scrub          exec.Scrub
	ProtectedPaths *protect.Set
	Registry       *cli.Catalog
	Search         bool
	Inputs         []poo.Modality
	CodemodeEngine string
	ToolNames      []string
	Offered        cli.Offerings
	MCP            []MCPRunning
}
```

- The map key is the name used by profiles, permission rules, and the wire protocol, and must match `Spec().Name`.
- `ToolNames` lists the tools the session offers so refusal messages only reference tools the model can actually call.
- `Offered` exposes the live snapshot of registered CLI commands and running MCP server tools.
- `MCP` holds the session's started MCP servers in selection order (empty at build time; populated when a session starts its servers).

For tools with pluggable engines such as `codemode`, wire the engine you link inside the factory:

```go
"codemode": func(config.ToolOptions) poo.Tool {
	return codemode.New(starlark.New())
},
```

Unlinking a tool removes its schema and its prompt section from the binary entirely. To omit a linked tool per project without rebuilding, use `tools.disabled` in settings. Note that `poo/config` does not import any tool package, so settings files still decode and validate even when a tool is not linked.

## Custom prompt directories (`PromptFS`)

Each built-in prompt section lives in an embedded markdown file beside the package that owns it. A custom binary can override any section by embedding a directory and passing it via `server.Options.PromptFS` (or `config.BuildOptions.PromptFS` when calling `config.Build` directly):

```go
//go:embed prompts
var promptDir embed.FS

prompts, err := fs.Sub(promptDir, "prompts")
if err != nil {
	return err
}
srv, err := server.New(server.Options{
	// ...
	PromptFS: prompts,
})
```

### Directory layout and section names

Files are named after the sections in `prompt.Order()` (`base`, `profile`, `catalog`, `environment`, `project`) and `tools.<tool>` for tool-owned sections. Subdirectories represent dot prefixes, and variants are sibling files with a variant suffix:

```text
prompts/
  base.md
  profile.md
  environment.md
  tools/bash.md
  tools/bash.small-local.md
```

- `profile.md` replaces a profile's own `profile.Profile.Prompt` prose (rendered immediately after `base`).
- A default section file (e.g. `tools/bash.md`) replaces the default text while preserving any embedded variants not explicitly overridden.
- Unknown section names or non-markdown files fail on load, naming the offending file.
- A linked tool's section loads for all profiles, but only profiles offering that tool render it.

### Templates and validation

Each markdown file is parsed as a Go `text/template` and receives the same data struct as the section it replaces:

- `environment.md`: `{{.Cwd}}`, `{{.OS}}`, `{{.Date}}`, `{{.Model}}`
- `catalog.md`: `{{.Search}}` (bool), `{{.Count}}` (int), `{{.Call}}`, `{{.Find}}`, and `{{.Entries}}` (`{{.Name}}`, `{{.Description}}`)
- `tools/jobs.md`: `{{.Feeds}}` (`{{.Name}}`, `{{.Description}}`)

A single trailing newline at EOF is stripped during rendering; an extra blank line preserves a trailing newline.

Templates are syntax-checked at load time and rendered when a session is constructed (or reconfigured with a new model or variant). A render failure prevents session creation (`config.Error` with code `invalid_value` on `system_prompt` in CLI mode, or `invalid_settings` on `session/create` over the wire). On `session/configure`, a render error rejects the change and leaves the session unchanged.

### Prompt layer precedence

Layers apply in order, with later layers winning:

1. Embedded defaults
2. Binary's `PromptFS` directory
3. Settings (`system_prompt.*`, CLI `--system-prompt` / `--append-system-prompt`)
4. User instructions (`BuildOptions.UserPromptFile` / `session.user_prompt_file`, process-wide)
5. Project instructions (`AGENTS.md`, read per session from the session's working directory)

`system_prompt.replace` clears the `PromptFS` sections; if the session offers registry tools, the embedded catalog section is restored after replacement. The [Skills](/capabilities/skills) catalog is a separate section rendered between `catalog` and `environment`. See [Profiles & Prompts](/configuration/profiles-and-prompts) for operator-level prompt settings.

## Custom executors (`poo/exec`)

Tools that run subprocesses (`bash`, `call_cli`, feeds) never spawn OS processes directly—they delegate to an `exec.Executor`:

```go
type Executor interface {
	Name() string
	Start(ctx context.Context, c Command, out io.Writer) (Process, error)
}

type Process interface {
	Wait() (exitCode int, err error)
	Kill()
	Stopped() bool
}
```

`exec.Command` carries `Argv`, `Dir`, scrubbed `Env`, optional `*string` `Stdin`, and optional `Stderr` (when `nil`, stdout and stderr are merged into `out`). When `ctx` is cancelled, the executor must stop the command and its process tree, and `Stopped()` must report `true` after `Wait()` returns. If `Stdin` cannot be written completely before the child exits, `Wait()` reports `exec.ErrStdinIncomplete` alongside the exit error (unless the command was stopped).

Register custom executors in an `exec.Registry` and pass it to `server.Options.Executors`:

```go
registry := exec.NewRegistry()
registry.Register("my-sandbox", func(opts exec.Options) (exec.Executor, error) {
	return newMySandbox(opts.Masker, opts.Sandbox)
})
```

`exec.Options` supplies `Masker` (for expanding protected paths to mask inside mounts) and `Sandbox` (`Network`, `ROBinds`, `RWBinds`). See [Sandboxing (bwrap)](/operations/sandbox) for the built-in Linux bubblewrap implementation.

---

<!-- Source: extending/wire-protocol.md -->

# Wire Protocol

`poo serve` exposes a JSON-RPC 2.0 control protocol over stdin and stdout, framed as one JSON object per line (NDJSON). The public contract lives in `poo/wire/protocol`.

## Handshake (`poo/initialize`)

`poo/initialize` must be the first request on the stream. Calling any other method before the handshake succeeds returns JSON-RPC error `-32002` (`data.code: "not_initialized"`).

The client sends its supported `protocol_versions` (currently `[1]`), name, version, and `capabilities`:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"poo/initialize","params":{"protocol_versions":[1],"client":{"name":"my-client","version":"0.1.0","capabilities":{"permission_answers":true}}}}
```

If no protocol version is shared, the server returns `-32001` (`protocol_version_unsupported`). On success, the server returns the negotiated version, `build` metadata, `capabilities` (`decider`, `compaction`, `persistence`, `jobs`, `feeds`, `history_origin`), `profiles`, `default_profile`, and `roles`.

::: info Client capability: `permission_answers`
Only a client that declares `capabilities.permission_answers: true` receives `permission/ask` requests from the server. Clients that omit it are never asked—every ask falls back immediately, and `session/create` / `session/load` report a warning.
:::

## Strict parameter decoding

Every method decodes its `params` object strictly via `protocol.DecodeParams`:

- Omitting an optional field selects its default.
- Passing an explicit `null` for `params` or any field returns `-32602` with `data.code: "invalid_params"`.
- Passing an unrecognized field at any nesting depth returns `-32602` with `data.code: "unknown_field"`.

## Session methods

| Method | Purpose | Key behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `session/create` | Create a new session | Requires `working_dir`. Optional `mode` must be in the handshake's `capabilities.persistence`. Response is queued before the event observer attaches, so no event arrives before the client learns `session_id`. |
| `session/load` | Open a recorded session | Requires `session_id`. Recovers torn tails, reports `recovered_tail`, `interrupted_runs`, `warnings`, and any `pending_run` on durable sessions. |
| `session/resume_run` | Continue a durable session's pending run | Starts the pending run asynchronously and returns `{"run_id": "..."}`. Returns `no_pending_run` or `busy` when not applicable. |
| `session/get` | Inspect current session state | Returns FSM `state`, `run_id`, active `jobs`, rendered `prompt` state, `reasoning`, `broken`, `pending_run`, and `awaiting` status. |
| `session/configure` | Update session settings between runs | Refused with `busy` while a run is active. Re-renders the system prompt if model or variant changes; rejects and preserves prior state on template error. |
| `session/history` | Page recorded session history | Accepts `session_id`, optional `before_seq`, and `limit` (capped at `poo.MaxHistoryLimit`). Pages backwards; returns `items` oldest-first and `has_more`. |
| `session/close` | Close a session and release locks | Cancels active work, stops feeds/jobs/MCP servers, closes the store, and returns `{}`. |

## Run, job, and catalog methods

| Method | Purpose | Key behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `run/prompt` | Start a new run | Requires `session_id` and `text` (optional `delivered` metadata). Returns `{"run_id": "..."}` immediately; watch progress via `event` notifications or `run/inspect`. |
| `run/message` | Send input to an active run | Requires `session_id` and `text`. `mode` is `"steer"` (default), `"interrupt"`, or `"follow_up"`. Returns `{"input_id": "..."}`. |
| `run/inspect` | Poll events and optionally wait for settle | Accepts `after_seq` and optional `wait: {"until": "settled", "run_id": "...", "timeout_ms": ...}` (default 30s). Returns `events`, `next_seq`, `has_more`, `state`, and `settled` or `timed_out: true`. |
| `run/cancel` | Cancel an active run | Requires `session_id` and `run_id`. Idempotent for already-settled runs; returns `run_not_found` for unknown IDs. |
| `run/background` | Move a live tool call to a background job | Requires `session_id`, `run_id`, and `handle`. Returns `{"job": "..."}` or `call_not_backgroundable`. |
| `job/cancel` | Stop a background job or feed | Requires `session_id` and `job` (e.g. `j1` or `feed:inbox`). Idempotent for unknown or finished jobs. |
| `models/list` | Return the effective model catalog | Accepts optional `refresh: true`. Returns `{"models": [...]}`. |
| `settings/get` | Return effective merged settings | Returns the post-override settings object. |

## Server notifications and requests

### Event notifications (`event`)

The server pushes every session event as a JSON-RPC notification with `method: "event"`. `protocol.Event` marshals as a flat JSON object containing `session_id`, session-monotonic `seq`, `type`, `at`, and the event's own fields:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"event","params":{"session_id":"01J...","seq":4,"type":"message.delta","at":"2026-01-01T00:00:00Z","run_id":"r1","text":"hello"}}
```

Event types cover the full lifecycle:

- **Runs & turns**: `run.started`, `run.settling`, `run.settled`, `turn.started`, `turn.ended`, `turn.interrupted`, `message.delta`, `provider.retry`
- **Inputs**: `input.queued`, `input.delivered`, `input.dropped`, `input.held`
- **Tools & permissions**: tool call/result events and permission ask/decision events
- **Jobs & feeds**: `job.started`, `job.ended`, `feed.started`, `feed.ended`

Clients should ignore unknown event types for forward compatibility within protocol version 1.

### Permission asks (`permission/ask`)

Unlike `event` notifications, a permission ask is a **server-initiated JSON-RPC request** with an `id` equal to `params.ask_id`:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"ask-1","method":"permission/ask","params":{"session_id":"01J...","run_id":"r1","ask_id":"ask-1","tool":"bash","summary":"rm -rf build","class":"side_effecting","reason":"policy"}}
```

For doom-loop asks, `reason` is `"doom_loop"` and `repeat_count` includes `exact` and `near` counts. The client responds with the matching `id` and a `protocol.AskResult`:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"ask-1","result":{"decision":"allow"}}
```

`decision` must be `"allow"` or `"deny"`. An optional `message` string on a denial is shown to the model in the tool result and recorded in the session log.

## `poo/wire/protocol` package

`poo/wire/protocol` imports only the Go standard library so external Go clients can depend on the wire contract without importing `poo` or any of its runtime packages. It exports:

- Envelope types: `Request`, `Response`, `Notification`, `Error`, `ErrorData`
- Method constants (`MethodInitialize`, `MethodSessionCreate`, `MethodRunPrompt`, `MethodPermissionAsk`, `MethodEvent`, etc.)
- Parameter and result DTOs for every method, plus `Event` with symmetric flat `MarshalJSON`/`UnmarshalJSON`
- JSON-RPC error codes (`-32700` to `-32603`, `-32000` `CodeServerError`, `-32001` `CodeVersionUnsupported`, `-32002` `CodeNotInitialized`)
- Machine-readable `ErrorData.Code` constants (`session_not_found`, `session_locked`, `busy`, `invalid_settings`, `unknown_model`, `unknown_profile`, `unknown_field`, etc.)—clients should branch on `error.data.code` rather than parsing `error.message`

When embedding `wire.Serve`, transport backpressure and teardown limits are configurable via `wire.Bounds` (defaults: 10,000 queued messages, 16 MiB queue bytes, 10s write stall, 5s drain).

---

<!-- Source: extending/conformance-and-testing.md -->

# Conformance & Testing

Poo ships two exported testing packages: `poo/wire/conformance` for black-box protocol verification and client integration tests against real binaries, and `poo/pootest` for in-process Go unit tests against `poo.Session`.

## Wire conformance suite (`poo/wire/conformance`)

`poo/wire/conformance` is a black-box test suite. It launches a compiled binary with a temporary settings file pointing at a local fake OpenAI-compatible endpoint. It then drives the binary strictly over stdin and stdout. It imports only the Go standard library and `poo/wire/protocol`.

```go
func TestMyBinarySpeaksTheProtocol(t *testing.T) {
	report := conformance.Run(t, conformance.Target{
		Binary:  binary,
		Args:    []string{"serve"},
		Profile: "search",
		Env:     []string{"MY_POO_ID=conformance"},
	})
	if len(report.Skipped) > 0 {
		t.Logf("skipped: %v", report.Skipped)
	}
}
```

### Target requirements

- `Target.Binary` must be a compiled executable path (build your command before calling `conformance.Run`).
- The suite passes `--settings <file>` on every invocation and `--ephemeral` for the ephemeral-session flow, so your binary must accept both flags.
- `Target.Profile` must name a profile the binary announces in `poo/initialize` (defaults to `"code"` when empty).
- `Target.Env` appends child-only environment variables (useful for binaries that require an identity or socket path) without mutating the test process's environment.
- `Target.Fixtures` lets you supply custom `ScriptedAnswer` turns, model name, and context limit to exercise tools unique to your binary.

### Adaptive flows and forward compatibility

Flows adapt to what the binary announces in its handshake:

- Bash-scripting flows run only when `bash` is offered.
- Typed-result flows run only when `finish` is offered.
- Feed flows run only when `capabilities.feeds` is `true`.

`conformance.Run` returns a `Report` listing the flows that ran and any that were skipped. A full-featured binary can assert `len(report.Skipped) == 0` in CI.

Responses are decoded under the protocol's forward-compatibility rules. Unexpected fields on known DTOs fail the test unless covered by an announced capability. Unknown capability keys and unknown event types are tolerated.

## Fake endpoint for client tests (`conformance.NewFakeEndpoint`)

Wire clients can test against a real `poo` binary without running the full conformance suite by importing `conformance.NewFakeEndpoint`:

```go
endpoint := conformance.NewFakeEndpoint(
	conformance.ScriptedAnswer{Text: "hello from poo"},
	conformance.ScriptedAnswer{ToolCalls: []conformance.ToolCall{
		{Name: "bash", Arguments: map[string]any{"command": "echo hi"}},
	}},
)
defer endpoint.Close()

settings := filepath.Join(dir, "settings.json")
if err := endpoint.WriteSettings(settings, "conformance-model", 32768, nil); err != nil {
	return err
}
// Launch the binary with `--settings settings` and drive it over stdio.
```

`ScriptedAnswer` supports:

- `Text`: complete assistant reply text.
- `Chunks`: explicit delta chunks for testing streaming behavior.
- `ToolCalls`: ordered `conformance.ToolCall` entries (`Name`, `Arguments`).
- `Status` and `Error`: HTTP status and `ProviderError` body for rate-limit and error-handling tests.
- `Delay`: artificial latency before responding (useful for testing `run/message` interrupts or `run/cancel`).
- `FailAfterDelta`: emit initial text then break the stream mid-response.

When scripted turns are exhausted, the endpoint repeats its final turn so clients do not need to script every follow-up request. Call `endpoint.RequestBodies()` to inspect the exact HTTP request bodies the binary sent in order, and `endpoint.Close()` when finished.

## In-process test helpers (`poo/pootest`)

`poo/pootest` exports in-process test doubles for Go unit tests that construct a `poo.Session` directly. It imports only `poo`, `poo/decide`, and the standard library.

### Scripted transport (`pootest.Transport`)

`pootest.Transport` implements `poo.ChatTransport` over a fixed sequence of `pootest.Turn` values (`Text`, `Thinking`, `Calls`, `Finish`, token counts, `Blocks`, `Err`, and mid-stream `Fail`).

- Unlike `FakeEndpoint`, `pootest.Transport` returns `pootest.ErrScriptExhausted` when turns run out so a one-turn test fails fast instead of looping.
- Supports recording every `poo.ChatRequest` and rendered prompt snapshot, scripting fork turns (for compaction or sub-requests), and scripting native compaction responses.

### In-memory record sink (`pootest.Sink`)

`pootest.NewSink()` provides a thread-safe, in-memory `poo.RecordSink` and `ReadRecords` reader:

- Stamps sequence numbers and timestamps onto every accepted `poo.Record`.
- `WaitRecords(ctx, name, n)` blocks until at least `n` records of type `name` are recorded (avoiding polling loops in tests).
- `FailAt(n)` and `SetError(err)` inject store write failures on the *n*-th append (defaulting to `pootest.ErrSinkFailed`).

### Stub decider (`pootest.StubDecider`)

`pootest.NewStubDecider(probability)` implements `decide.Decider`, assigning `probability` to the first option of each question and splitting the remainder evenly across the rest:

- `SetChoice(name)` pins the returned choice; `SetError(err)` injects decision failures.
- `Calls()`, `Questions()`, and `States()` inspect every decision request made during the test.
- Pair with `pootest.NewRecordingSink()` to capture `decide.Decision` records.

### Scripted compactor (`pootest.Compactor`)

`pootest.NewCompactor(should, compaction)` implements `poo.Compactor` with a fixed decision and compaction payload:

- `SetShouldAfter(turns)` delays returning `true` from `ShouldCompact` until the view has at least `turns` turns.
- `SetError(err)` injects compaction errors.
- `Fork` and `ForkJSON` call the session's `poo.ForkFunc` while recording `ForkCall` arguments; `Calls()`, `Views()`, and `Forks()` inspect all invocations.

---

<!-- Source: extending/prior-art.md -->

# Prior Art

`poo` builds on concrete ideas from earlier agent harnesses and deliberately rejects others. This page records what was studied, what `poo` adopted, and where it diverges.

## `mini-swe-agent`

- **Source:** [SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent)
- **Version studied:** `v2.4.6` (`04d809ceab9df28f9adaed044884180159172930`)
- **Areas studied:** default and interactive agent loops, local shell execution, exception control flow, YAML config templates, and tool-call parsing.

### Adopted

- **Bash as the primary verb.** `mini-swe-agent` treats shell execution as the main way to act on a repo. `poo` keeps `bash` central in the `code` [profile](/configuration/profiles-and-prompts) and adds `read`, `grep`, `edit`, and `write` so read-only binaries can omit `bash` entirely.
- **Stateless shell per call.** Every command runs in a fresh subshell; `cd` and exported variables do not persist across calls. `poo`'s system prompt states this contract explicitly.
- **Linear, append-only history.** Nothing rewrites the model's view of history silently. Compaction always writes a visible replacement and leaves the session store intact.
- **Observation envelope with head/tail elision.** Above a context-relative cap, `poo` renders the head and tail of command output with an elision count. The envelope hints at `grep`, `sed`, `head`, or `tail` to inspect smaller slices.
- **Section-based prompt structure.** `poo` splits the operating contract, tool rules, and environment context into named [prompt sections](/configuration/profiles-and-prompts). It keeps `mini-swe-agent`'s shell guidance while using native tool calls where supported.
- **Process-group kill on timeout.** Timed-out commands kill their entire process group (with a grace period before `SIGKILL`) so no orphaned child processes survive.

### Rejected

- **Bash as the only tool.** Read-only builds cannot link `bash` at all, so file inspection needs dedicated read-only tools.
- **Magic-string completion.** Instead of ending a run when stdout prints a sentinel string, `poo` provides the typed, schema-validated [`finish` tool](/capabilities/tools-and-jobs).
- **Exception-driven control flow.** `poo` uses an explicit [session FSM](/extending/architecture) with a closed [settle-reason enum](/operations/limits-and-exit-codes). The [wire protocol](/extending/wire-protocol), `run/inspect`, and session replay all depend on a known state set.
- **Format-error retry counters.** `poo` returns malformed tool calls to the model as recoverable validation errors and bounds retries with `max_continuations`.
- **Control messages inside the transcript.** `poo` keeps the message list to model and tool turns and records control outcomes as typed [session log records](/reference/session-log-v0).
- **Heavy core dependencies.** `poo`'s core packages (`poo`, `poo/prompt`, `poo/decide`, `poo/wire/protocol`) depend only on the Go standard library, enforced by `internal/depcheck`. Opt-in packages (such as the [REPL](/getting-started/repl), SQLite store, and QuickJS engine) carry their own dependencies only when linked.

## `pi-durable`

- **Source:** ["Pi Durable"](https://earendil.com/posts/pi-durable/) (Earendil Engineering, October 2026)
- **Areas studied:** storage backends, single-owner locking, durable tasks, prompt sections, extensions, forks, and compaction.

### Adopted

- **Single-owner storage authority.** `poo` supports JSONL and SQLite [session stores](/operations/sessions-and-durability) and enforces single-process ownership via file locks and lease TTLs.
- **Session-to-run lifecycle.** A session holds a sequence of runs (one active run at a time) behind a clean store, projection, and authority seam.
- **Write-ahead durability.** `poo` writes every record as it happens. Loading a `logged` session marks any interrupted run; loading a `durable` session plans and resumes the run from the interrupted phase.
- **Section-based prompts.** Like `pi-durable`, `poo` assembles prompts from named sections. Unlike `pi-durable`, `poo` freezes the rendered prompt for the length of a run so provider prompt caches stay valid.
- **Structured tool-call records.** Every tool call is recorded with its intent and outcome as it runs.
- **Transport-level prefix forks.** [Compaction strategies](/capabilities/compaction) (`mine`, `pointer`, `handoff`) fork the last main request byte-for-byte to reuse the provider's prompt cache without creating a separate conversation branch.
- **Handoff notes.** `poo`'s `handoff` compaction strategy mirrors `pi-durable`'s `reset(note)` pattern as an opt-in strategy alongside the default `mine` strategy.

### Rejected

- **Task graphs and subagent trees.** `poo` runs one agent loop per session with no built-in subagent tree. Multi-agent orchestration belongs to an external supervisor (such as Avenor via [feeds](/capabilities/feeds-and-daemon) or [MCP](/capabilities/mcp-servers)).
- **First-class forked conversations.** Sessions remain linear; forks exist only at the transport layer for compaction passes.
- **Runtime-mutable extension registries.** `poo` composes Go extensions at compile time via [`server.New`](/extending/custom-binary). For no-rebuild extensibility, operators drop in declarative [CLI registry](/capabilities/cli-registry) or [MCP](/capabilities/mcp-servers) manifests instead of mutating a running registry.
- **Automatic tool replay policies.** `poo` does not tag tools `replay: "safe"` to re-run them automatically after a crash. Recovery records an interrupted outcome so the caller or durable planner can continue safely.
- **Typed application-state documents.** `poo` has no built-in document store for plans or todos.
- **Silent background compaction.** Compaction never rewrites history behind the model's back. Every strategy writes a visible replacement and leaves stored history intact.

## Related Pages

- [Why `poo`?](/getting-started/why-poo) — core philosophy and extensibility ladder
- [Architecture](/extending/architecture) — package boundaries, FSM states, and hooks
- [Context Compaction](/capabilities/compaction) — compaction strategies and transparent history
- [Sessions & Durability](/operations/sessions-and-durability) — JSONL/SQLite stores, leases, and crash recovery
