| `summary` | string | The call's human-facing summary, as the `tool.call` event shows it. A bash call shows the model's `description`, or the command when it supplied none. **Absent** when the tool has no summary, and on a log written before the field existed. |
| `arguments` | object or string | The full arguments, in the same shape as a `tool_call` content block. The reserved `background` argument is kept here, even though the core removes it before the tool sees it. |
| `mode` | string | How the call ran: `"sync"` in the turn, `"job"` in the background, or `"nested"` from inside another call. Absent when the log was written before the field existed. |
| `parent` | string | The handle of the call that made this one, for a call a running tool made through the nested seam. The model-made call a script ran under, so a reader can walk the calls one script made. **Absent** on a call the model made. A nested call that never ran carries the parent and no `mode`, like any other call that did not run. |

A nested call's result is recorded but never becomes a `message`: the
model never saw the call, and the log's contract — the messages in the
log are the same list the model sees — keeps holding. It goes back to
the tool that made the call instead, after the same before-tool and
after-tool hooks a model-made call goes through. The recovery's message
rule leaves a call that names a `parent` out of the history, so a torn
tail's nested calls are closed without polluting it either.

A nested call's tool runs under a cap of 1,048,576 characters
(`poo.NestedOutputCapChars`) and not the session's context-relative
caps, since its output never reaches the model directly. The tool that
made the call reads the whole result. The record's `text` and the
`tool.result` event's `text` are held to the session's observation cap,
with the rest counted in `elided_chars`. A cut `text` ends with a line
that says how many more characters went to the calling tool. A hook's
replaced original is cut the same way.

The record's `structured` payload is kept whole, so a tool whose
payload holds its output has that output in the log once. Bash's
capture always fits under the nested cap. `call_cli`'s stdout and
stderr share the cap, so two streams that pass it together are kept
as their heads and tails. A tool with no payload, such as read or
grep, has only the cut text.

## `tool.result`

The outcome of a tool call.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `run_id` | string | The run the result belongs to. |
| `turn` | integer | The turn the result belongs to. |
| `handle` | string | The call's handle within the turn. |
| `tool` | string | The tool that ran. |
| `outcome` | string | `"ok"`, `"error"`, `"denied"`, `"skipped"`, `"cancelled"`, `"interrupted"` or `"started"`. |
| `text` | string | The model-facing text of the result. A nested call's text is held to the session's observation cap. |
| `elided_chars` | integer | The characters a nested call's `text` left out. Absent when the text is whole. |
| `structured` | any | The tool's side-channel payload. Absent when the tool has none. |
| `original` | object | The result the tool produced, when a hook replaced it. Absent when no hook replaced it, and absent for a redacted result: the original of a redacted result never reaches the log. |
| `redacted` | boolean | `true` when a hook redacted the result. Absent when it did not. |
| `redacted_by` | string | The name of the hook that redacted the result. Absent unless the result was redacted. |
| `hooks` | array of objects | The after-tool hooks' decisions, in the order the hooks ran. Absent when no hook acted. A redacted chain's decisions carry no `text`. |

`original` holds:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | string | The model-facing text of the result the tool produced. |
| `structured` | any | The tool's side-channel payload. Absent when the tool had none. |
| `is_error` | boolean | `true` when the result reported a failure. Absent when it did not. |

A `hooks` entry holds:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `hook` | string | The name of the hook that decided. |
| `action` | string | What the hook did: `"keep"`, `"annotate"`, `"replace"` or `"redact"`. |
| `text` | string | The text the hook added or substituted. Absent when the chain was redacted, and absent when the hook kept the result. |

An `error` outcome is recoverable: the model saw the text and the run
continued. A bash call that hit its timeout is an `error` outcome, because
the model has to see that the command failed rather than read its partial
output as a finished command.

The `started` outcome belongs to a background job: the call returned at
once and its result arrives later as a message. The `denied`, `skipped`,
`cancelled` and `interrupted` outcomes arrive with the later stages that
produce them.

An `interrupted` outcome is written by a load, never by a live run: the
call was cut short, its outcome is unknown, and the model is told so. The
result is the model-facing text of the call, and the message that carries
it answers the call the model made, so a session that is loaded again asks
the model nothing it cannot answer.

## `input.queued`

An input the session accepted. The record is written before the call
that accepted the input returns, so an accepted input is never lost: its
fate is in the records.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `session_id` | string | The session's identifier. |
| `run_id` | string | The run the input belongs to. Absent when the session had no run. |
| `input_id` | string | The input's identifier: a ULID. |
| `mode` | string | How the input is delivered: `"steer"`, `"interrupt"`, `"follow_up"` or `"feed"`. |
| `text` | string | The message text. |
| `attachments` | array of objects | The files the input carries, each holding `modality`, `media_type` and `data` (base64), so a held input survives a restart with what it carried. Absent when the input carries none. A feed's input carries its image this way. |
| `delivery_note` | object | How much of the previous reply the user had seen. Absent when the input carries none. Its `text` is empty when the reply was still streaming at acceptance; the delivered message carries the note rendered at delivery. |
| `data` | object | The object a feed's filter wrote beside the text, kept so a held input is still a structured record after a restart. Absent unless a filter produced one. |
| `queued_at` | string | RFC 3339, UTC. |

## `input.delivered`

An input that reached the model.

The `message` that delivers the input is the delivery's commit point:
once that record is in the log the input has reached the model, and a
store that refuses this record does not undo the delivery. The load
writes the missing record from the message.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `session_id` | string | The session's identifier. |
| `run_id` | string | The run the input was delivered to. |
| `input_id` | string | The input's identifier: a ULID. |
| `mode` | string | How the input was delivered: `"steer"`, `"interrupt"`, `"follow_up"`, `"job"` for a background job's result, or `"feed"` for a feed's input. |
| `delivered_at` | string | RFC 3339, UTC. |

## `input.dropped`

An input that never reached the model. The reason is the run's final
settle reason, or `backlog` when the feed's backlog cap dropped the
input with no run involved.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `session_id` | string | The session's identifier. |
| `run_id` | string | The run the input belonged to. Absent when the session had no run. |
| `input_id` | string | The input's identifier: a ULID. |
| `mode` | string | How the input was accepted. |
| `reason` | string | Why the input was dropped. |
| `dropped_at` | string | RFC 3339, UTC. |

## `input.held`

Job results that were held instead of delivered. A held result waits
for the next run, or for the next load: it is never lost.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `session_id` | string | The session's identifier. |
| `run_id` | string | The run the results were held for. Absent when the session had no run. |
| `jobs` | array of strings | The jobs whose results were held, or the feeds whose inputs were held. A feed's entry is its origin, e.g. `"feed:inbox"`. |
| `reason` | string | Why they were held: `"on_idle"`, `"wake_limit"` or `"session_closed"`. |
| `held_at` | string | RFC 3339, UTC. |

## `job.started`

A background job was accepted and started. The record is the
acceptance: the job, the call it came from, the run that started it and
the tool it runs.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `session_id` | string | The session's identifier. |
| `job` | string | The job's identifier, e.g. `"j3"`. |
| `handle` | string | The handle of the tool call the job came from, e.g. `"r1"`. The call returned at once with a `"started"` outcome. |
| `tool` | string | The name of the tool the job runs. |
| `run_id` | string | The run that started the job. |
| `started_at` | string | RFC 3339, UTC. |

## `job.ended`

A background job finished. The record carries the result the model
reads, so a held result survives a crash and a load can deliver it.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `session_id` | string | The session's identifier. |
| `job` | string | The job's identifier, e.g. `"j3"`. |
| `handle` | string | The handle of the tool call the job came from. |
| `tool` | string | The name of the tool the job ran. |
| `run_id` | string | The run that started the job. |
| `outcome` | string | How the job ended: `"ok"`, `"error"`, `"cancelled"` or `"interrupted"`. |
| `cause` | string | Why the job ended, when something else ended it. Absent unless the cause is `"session_closed"`. |
| `timed_out` | boolean | `true` when the job hit the jobs timeout. Absent when it did not. |
| `fatal` | boolean | `true` when the job failed with a fatal error. A run that receives the result settles `tool_fatal`. Absent when the job did not. |
| `input_id` | string | The id the queued result is delivered under. |
| `text` | string | The result the model reads. |
| `attachments` | array of objects | The files the result carries, each holding `modality`, `media_type` and `data` (base64), so a held result survives a restart with what it carried. Absent when the result carries none. An earlier build wrote this field as `images`, holding only `media_type` and `data`; a reader takes those as images. |
| `ended_at` | string | RFC 3339, UTC. |

## `feed.started`

One attempt of a feed started. A feed is a long-lived source that pushes
messages into a session, and the session owns its lifecycle: this record
names the attempt.

One instance's attempts never overlap, so the attempt's end is the next
`feed.ended` of the same origin. The `origin` is the instance's: the feed's
own `"feed:<name>"`, or `"feed:<name>[<field>=<value>]"` for an instance the
model started with `subscribe_feed`.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `session_id` | string | The session's identifier. |
| `feed` | string | The feed's name, e.g. `"inbox"`. The `origin` names the instance. |
| `attempt` | integer | The attempt's number within the session and the instance, counting from 1. A loaded session carries on past the numbers the log holds, except an optional feed a subscription started: a restored session holds no optional instances, so a re-subscribed one restarts at attempt 1. |
| `started_at` | string | RFC 3339, UTC. |

## `feed.ended`

One attempt of a feed ended. The record is terminal: the attempt is
never resumed, and a feed's failure reaches the model through the record
and the event, never as a message. A loaded session starts the feed's
next attempt under the next number, and a subscription's instance does not
start again on its own.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `session_id` | string | The session's identifier. |
| `feed` | string | The feed's name. |
| `attempt` | integer | The attempt's number within the session. |
| `outcome` | string | How the attempt ended: `"exited"`, `"failed"`, `"cancelled"`, `"suspended"`, `"session_closed"` or `"interrupted"`. |
| `error` | string | The runner's error, when it returned one. Absent when it did not. |
| `restart_in_ms` | integer | How long the session waits before the next attempt, in whole milliseconds, rounded up. Absent when no restart is scheduled. |
| `ended_at` | string | RFC 3339, UTC. |

`exited` means the runner returned without an error, and `failed` means
it returned an error or panicked. `cancelled` means `cancel_job` stopped
the attempt, and `session_closed` means the session closed under it, or
its store broke. `interrupted` is written by a load, never by a live
session: the process stopped during the attempt.

`suspended` means the feed's filter failed closed: the filter exited
nonzero, or wrote something other than a record, so the attempt ended and
the feed did not restart, whatever its restart policy says. The `error`
names the fault.

A suspension wakes the session with a `feed` input of its own, and that
input is the report of how the feed went down. Its text is the feed's
`<feed>` element with `fault` and `log` attributes beside `name`: the
fault's code, and the path of a file beside the session's own that holds
the filter's diagnostics for the attempt. Those diagnostics never ride the
input. One suspension is one wake: a further fault that arrives before the
report is delivered joins it, and the report counts it.

## `tool.started`

A side-effecting tool call started. The record is written before the
tool runs, so a durable session sees the effect a crash cut short and may
replay it. A read-only call writes none: it changes nothing to replay.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `run_id` | string | The run the call belongs to. |
| `turn` | integer | The turn the call belongs to. |
| `handle` | string | The call's handle within the turn, e.g. `"r1"`. |
| `call_id` | string | The provider's id of the call. The id the call answers, so a reader pairs the start with the call and the result by it. |
| `tool` | string | The name of the tool the call names. |

## `run.resumed`

A run resumed after a crash. The record names the phase the run stopped
in, so a reader of the log sees where the run picked up.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `run_id` | string | The run that resumed. |
| `resumption_attempt` | integer | The resumption's number, counting from 1. |
| `from_phase` | string | The phase the run was in when it stopped: one of the session's states, e.g. `"executing"`. |
| `turn` | integer | The turn the run was in when it stopped. |

## `turn.hook`

A turn hook's start or end. The record is written when the hook starts
and when it ends, so a reader of the log sees a hook that a crash cut
short: its start has no end, and its end may say it was interrupted.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `run_id` | string | The run the hook belongs to. |
| `turn` | integer | The turn the hook runs in. |
| `phase` | string | The hook's phase: `"after_turn"` or `"before_settle"`. |
| `status` | string | The record's status: `"started"`, `"ended"`, or `"skipped"` for a hook a resumed turn left out because it is not safe to run twice. |
| `hook_index` | integer | The hook's position in the chain, counting from 0. |
| `interrupted` | boolean | `true` when the hook's turn was ended by an interrupt. Set on the hook's records along the interrupted path, so a crash between them keeps the fact on the started record. Absent when it was not. |

## `feed.subscribed`

A feed instance subscribed. The record is written before the instance
runs, so a reader of the log sees the instances a session ran, and a
durable session knows which to take on again and the scope and prompt to
take them on with. A call that sets a prompt on a running instance writes
the record again, so the last one is the subscription the session would
repeat.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `feed` | string | The feed's name, e.g. `"inbox"`. |
| `instance` | string | The instance's identifier. |
| `scope` | string | The instance's scope. |
| `prompt` | string | The prompt the instance was started with. Absent when the instance was started without one. |

## `feed.unsubscribed`

A feed instance unsubscribed. The record is written when the instance
unsubscribes, so a reader of the log sees the instances a session let
go, and a durable session does not take them on again.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `feed` | string | The feed's name, e.g. `"inbox"`. |
| `instance` | string | The instance's identifier. |

## `observer.dropped`

The events an observer missed. The record is written at most once a
second per observer, so an observer that fell behind does not flood the
log, and it is never delivered to an observer: the diagnostics must not
cause more overflow.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `session_id` | string | The session's identifier. |
| `observer` | string | The observer that fell behind. |
| `count` | integer | How many events the observer missed. |
| `dropped_at` | string | RFC 3339, UTC. |

## `turn.interrupted`

A turn an interrupt cut short. The record follows the turn's end: a
client reads it as a note on the turn that just closed.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `session_id` | string | The session's identifier. |
| `run_id` | string | The run the turn belongs to. |
| `turn` | integer | The turn that was interrupted. |
| `input_ids` | array of strings | The inputs whose messages aborted the turn. |
| `interrupted_at` | string | RFC 3339, UTC. |

## `compaction`

What a compactor did. The store keeps every original record, and the
compaction record says what the model's view was replaced with.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `run_id` | string | The run the compaction belongs to. |
| `strategy` | string | The strategy that produced the compaction. |
| `compaction` | object | The compaction itself. Its shape is the strategy's form: `replace`, `rewrite`, `window` or `end`. |

## `usage`

The token accounting of one provider request. Every request whose stream
started gets a record, so a consumer can see the time to the first token
even when the endpoint reports no token counts.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `run_id` | string | The run the request belongs to. |
| `turn` | integer | The turn the request belongs to. |
| `request` | integer | The request's number within the run, starting at 1. `0` for a request a compaction made, which is not one of the run's turns. |
| `input_tokens` | integer | The prompt tokens the endpoint reported. `0` when it reported none. |
| `output_tokens` | integer | The completion tokens the endpoint reported. `0` when it reported none. |
| `cache_read_tokens` | integer | The prompt tokens served from the provider's cache. **Absent** when the endpoint does not report it. |
| `ttft_ms` | number | The time to the first streamed token, in milliseconds. Measured by the transport, not reported by the endpoint. |
| `origin` | string | Absent for the run's own turn. `compaction` when a compaction strategy made the request: a fork that wrote a handoff, or the request that wrote a summary. |

The time to the first token is the time to the first *token*: a non-empty
text delta, a thinking delta or a tool call. A chunk that only announces
the assistant's role carries no token, so it does not start the clock.

Every provider request whose stream started gets a `usage` record,
including a request whose stream failed part way through: the request
still cost tokens, and the record is what a consumer reads to account for
it. That includes the requests a compaction made, which carry the
compaction's origin so their share of the spend stays its own. A request
that failed before the endpoint's stream started has no usage record: no
token was spent on it. An endpoint that reports no usage for a request
writes no record either: the charge is an estimate, and the log holds
what the endpoint said.

## `provider.attempt`

One attempt of a provider request that failed. Every attempt is written,
the last one included, so a reader of the log sees what the request tried
and what each attempt failed with.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `run_id` | string | The run the request belongs to. |
| `turn` | integer | The turn the request belongs to. |
| `request` | integer | The request's number within the run, starting at 1. Every attempt record belongs to a turn's request. |
| `attempt` | integer | The attempt's number, counting from 1. |
| `error` | string | The failure's message. |
| `kind` | string | The provider error kind, when the failure is one. **Absent** when it is not. |
| `delay_ms` | integer | How long the transport waited before the next attempt. **Absent** when no retry followed. |

## `session.models_changed`

The session switched models. The switch happens between the runs, so a
reader of the log knows which model answered which turn.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `from` | string | The name of the model the session talked to. |
| `to` | string | The name of the model the session talks to now. |
| `warnings` | array of strings | What the caller should know about the switch. **Absent** when there was nothing to say. |
| `omitted` | array of objects | The provider blocks that are left out of the requests from now on, because they belong to another API. Each object holds `api`, `type` and `count`. **Absent** when nothing was left out. |

The history is never truncated by a switch. A view that does not fit the
new window is a warning, and the next run settles `context_exhausted`.

## `model.output_limit`

The session learned a model's output cap from an endpoint that rejected a
request whose `max_tokens` was above it. The session keeps the cap for the
requests that follow, and the record says why the value dropped.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `model_id` | string | The identifier of the model the endpoint rejected. |
| `previous` | integer | The `max_tokens` the rejected request asked for. |
| `limit` | integer | The `max_tokens` the endpoint accepts, which the session asks for from now on. |

A restored session applies the last record for the model it talks to,
unless that model declares its own limit.

## `decision`

One decision call. The record is written whatever the outcome was, so a
reader of the log sees the calls that could not be answered too.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `origin` | string | Who asked the questions. |
| `questions` | array of objects | The questions that were asked. Each holds `id`, `instructions` and its kind's own fields. |
| `state_hash` | string | The hex SHA-256 of the state payload the questions were asked about. |
| `answers` | array of objects | The answers, when the call succeeded. **Absent** when it did not. |
| `outcome` | string | `"ok"`, `"deferred"` or `"invalid"`. |
| `error` | string | The failure, when the call did not succeed. **Absent** when it did. |
| `latency_ms` | number | How long the call took, in milliseconds. |
| `requests` | integer | The number of wire requests the call made. **Absent** when the decider did not report one. |
| `at` | string | RFC 3339, UTC. |

## `permission.asked`

The ask a run is waiting on. The record is written when the run starts
waiting, before any asker has answered.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `run_id` | string | The run that is waiting. |
| `ask_id` | string | The ask's identifier. A client answers by it. |
| `tool` | string | The name of the tool the model called. |
| `summary` | string | What the call does, as the permission ask shows it. A bash call shows the command, never the model's `description`. **Absent** when the tool has no summary. |
| `class` | string | The tool's class: `"read_only"` or `"side_effecting"`. **Absent** when the tool names none. |
| `reason` | string | Why the call is being asked about: `"policy"` or `"doom_loop"`. **Absent** when there is none. |
| `repeat_count` | object | The doom loop's counts, for a doom-loop ask: `exact` and `near`. **Absent** for a policy ask. |
| `deadline` | string | The wall-clock time, RFC 3339 with nanosecond precision, when the ask expires. **Absent** when the ask has no deadline, and on a log written before the field existed. |
| `fallback` | string | The decision an expired ask resolves to: `"allow"` or `"deny"`. It is the request's effective fallback, so an ask that names none resolves to `"deny"`. **Absent** on a log written before the field existed. |

## `permission.answered`

The answer that resolved an ask. It follows its `permission.asked`, and it
is written whatever the decision was.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `run_id` | string | The run the answer belongs to. |
| `ask_id` | string | The ask the answer resolves. **Absent** for a doom loop's deterministic action, which answers no ask. |
| `decision` | string | `"allow"` or `"deny"`. |
| `answered_by` | string | Who answered: an asker, the chain's fallback, the policy's own action, or `"cancelled"` for a run that ended. |
| `provenance` | string | How the ask was resolved: `"answered"`, `"timeout"`, `"default"`, `"no_asker"`, `"cancelled"` or `"interrupted"`. |
| `reason` | string | Why the call was being asked about. **Absent** when there is none. |
| `message` | string | The note the answer carried for the model. For a policy ask the model saw it in the refused call's tool result; for a doom-loop ask the model sees the doom loop's own refusal text instead, and the record keeps the message. **Absent** when the answer carried none. |

## `run.settled`

The end of a run. It is the last record of a run.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `run_id` | string | The run's identifier: a ULID (26 characters of Crockford base32, the time first). |
| `reason` | string | The settle reason. See below. |
| `detail` | object | Why the run settled. |
| `turns` | integer | The number of provider requests the run made. |
| `settled_at` | string | RFC 3339, UTC. |

`detail` holds:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `source` | string | The condition that settled the run. |
| `text` | string | The human-readable explanation. Absent when there is none. |
| `losing` | array of strings | Other candidates that lost the precedence order. Absent when there were none. |
| `provider` | object | Set when a provider request failed. |
| `handoff` | string | The note a compactor wrote when it refused to compact. Absent when the run did not settle that way. |
| `undelivered_input` | array of objects | The accepted inputs that never reached the model. Absent when there were none. |
| `jobs_running` | array of strings | The jobs that were still running when the run settled. Absent when there were none. |
| `result` | any | The payload of a valid `finish` call, when the run settled as finished. Absent otherwise. |
| `usage` | object | The run's token accounting: the sum of what its requests reported. Absent when no request reported usage. |

A `usage` entry holds:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `input_tokens` | integer | The prompt tokens the requests reported, in total. |
| `output_tokens` | integer | The completion tokens the requests reported, in total. |
| `cache_read_tokens` | integer | The prompt tokens the providers served from their caches, in total. Absent when no request reported one. |

A `undelivered_input` entry holds:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `input_id` | string | The input's identifier: a ULID. |
| `mode` | string | How the input was accepted: `"steer"`, `"interrupt"` or `"follow_up"`. |

`provider` holds:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `kind` | string | The failure class, e.g. `"context_length"` or `"server"`. |
| `status` | integer | The HTTP status. Absent when the failure was not a response. |
| `code` | string | The provider's own error code. Absent when it sent none. It also holds the kind a failure had before it was reclassified: an `interrupted_stream` keeps the kind it broke in here. |
| `retry_after_s` | integer | How long the endpoint asked the client to wait, in seconds. Absent when it said nothing. |

### Settle reasons

The reasons are a closed set, and the exit code is the process's exit
code. The precedence is the order of the table: a run collects a
candidate from every source, and the highest-precedence one wins at the
commit point.

| Precedence | Reason | Exit | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `cancelled` | 130 | The run was cancelled. |
| 2 | `store_error` | 23 | The session's store failed. The session becomes broken. |
| 3 | `hook_error` | 22 | An executable hook failed or missed its deadline. |
| 4 | `tool_fatal` | 21 | A tool failed with an error that means the environment is unusable. |
| 5 | `provider_limit` | 24 | The provider refused for quota or plan reasons. The session is not broken. |
| 5b | `provider_error` | 20 | A provider request failed and cannot be retried, or the retry budget was spent. |
| 6 | `context_exhausted` | 13 | The context window is full. |
| 7 | `hook_continue_limit` | 12 | The `BeforeSettle` hooks asked for more continuations than the run allows. |
| 8 | `max_turns` | 11 | The run hit its turn limit. |
| 8b | `budget_exhausted` | 14 | The run hit a token or time budget. |
| 8c | `invalid_turns` | 15 | The model kept producing turns the run could not use: it asked for tool calls and sent none, or its calls did not parse, for as many consecutive turns as the run allows. |
| 9 | `finished` | 0 | The model called the `finish` tool with a valid result. |
| 9b | `stop_requested` | 0 | A hook or a stop condition asked the run to stop. |
| 10 | `output_truncated` | 10 | The provider stopped on the output-token limit. |
| 11 | `end_turn` | 0 | The model stopped on its own. |
| — | `interrupted` | — | The run's outcome is unknown: the process stopped while the run was going. It is never produced live; a load writes it for a run that never settled. |

`provider_limit` and `provider_error` share a precedence level, because
a single failed request produces only one of them.

A cancellation and a deadline are the same outcome: the run was stopped
before the model finished, and both settle `cancelled`.

`detail.source` names the condition. The values the core writes:

| Source | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `end_turn` | The model stopped on its own. |
| `output_truncated:default` | The provider stopped on the output-token limit, and the request carried poo's default for the model's context window, because the model declares no `max_output`. The detail's text names the `max_tokens` the request carried and the setting that raises it. |
| `output_truncated:model` | The provider stopped on the output-token limit, and the request carried the model's own `max_output`. |
| `output_truncated:context` | The provider stopped on the output-token limit, and the request carried the room the context window had left, which was under the model's output limit. The detail's text gives the estimated prompt size and the window. |
| `output_truncated:endpoint` | The provider stopped on the endpoint's own output limit: the request body carried no `max_tokens`, because the endpoint takes none. |
| `max_turns` | The run hit its turn limit. |
| `max_run_tokens` | The run hit its token budget. |
| `max_duration` | The run hit its wall-clock budget. |
| `empty_turns` | The model reached the bound on consecutive turns that asked for tool calls and sent none. The detail's text says how many turns. A run that mixed the two kinds of unusable turn is named for its last turn. |
| `unparsed_calls` | The model reached the bound on consecutive turns whose tool calls did not parse. The detail's text says how many turns. A run that mixed the two kinds of unusable turn is named for its last turn. |
| `truncated_turns` | The model reached the bound on consecutive turns whose response stopped on the output-token limit before a complete call arrived, with `limits.truncation_retries` retries already spent. The detail's text says how many turns. |
| `no_output_room` | The computed `max_tokens` was under 256, so the request was never sent. |
| `prompt_limit` | The estimate plus the reserve was over the endpoint's input cap, so the request was never sent. |
| `compaction_failed` | The compactor failed when the next request could not go out. |
| `provider:context_length` | The endpoint reported that the request was too long. It is recognised whatever status the endpoint sent it with, including a 5xx. The run compacts once and sends the request again when it has a compactor, the refused request carried no partial answer, and no interrupt is pending. A handoff strategy forks the refused request, which fails, so the run settles with the refusal. Without those conditions the run settles as before. |
| `provider:<kind>` | The provider request failed with that kind. |
| `finish` | The model called the `finish` tool with a valid result. |
| `before_settle` | A `BeforeSettle` hook stopped the run, or the run asked for more continuations than it allows. |
| `after_turn:<name>` | An `AfterTurn` hook stopped the run. |
| `stop_condition` | A stop condition matched. |
| `cancel:context` | The run's context was cancelled. |
| `cancel:deadline` | The run's context deadline passed. |
| `cancel:client` | The client cancelled the run. |
| `cancel:close` | The session closed while the run was active. |
| `store` | The session's store refused a record. |

## Reading a log

A consumer reads the file line by line and decodes each line as a JSON
object. It keys off `record`, and it must tolerate fields it does not
recognise: a later stage adds records and fields, and a consumer that
fails on an unknown field breaks on a newer log.

A log written by an earlier core is still readable. The fields added
after the first version are all optional: `message_id`, `input_id`,
`delivery_note` and `trigger` are absent from an older log, and a
consumer that needs them must treat an absent field as "the log does not
say".

The order of the records is the order of the events. A `tool.call` is
always followed by its `tool.result`, and a `run.started` is always
followed by a `run.settled`. One feed instance's attempts never overlap, so
a `feed.started` is followed by its `feed.ended` before that instance's
next `feed.started`. The core writes the settle record itself, so
a run that was cancelled, or whose provider failed, still ends with one.
Every record is written under a context of its own, bounded at 5 s, so a
cancelled run still records what it did. A `usage` record the store
refuses is dropped rather than ending the run. Only a store that refuses
the run's other records stops it before its `run.settled`.

## The tools' observations

A `tool.result` carries the tool's own text in `text`, and the tool's
side-channel payload in `structured`. The two tools the skeleton ships
have these shapes.

The bash tool's payload is the observation the model reads, as JSON:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `returncode` | integer or null | The command's exit status. Null when the process was killed, which is the case for a timeout. |
| `timed_out` | boolean | Whether the command hit its timeout. |
| `output` | string | The output, when it fits under the observation cap. |
| `output_head` | string | The head of the output, when it was elided. |
| `output_tail` | string | The tail of the output, when it was elided. |
| `elided_chars` | integer | The characters dropped from the middle. Absent when the output was not elided. |
| `truncated` | boolean | True when the output passed the 1 MiB capture and the rest was dropped. Absent otherwise. |
| `hint` | string | How to see the elided middle, or the dropped end when `truncated` is set. Absent when the output was neither elided nor truncated. |

The observation cap and `elided_chars` are counted in characters, not
bytes, and a cut never splits a rune. A byte that is not part of a valid
character counts as one character. The output is captured up to 1 MiB,
and a capture cut that lands in the middle of a character drops the
partial one. Bytes the command printed are otherwise kept as they are.

The read tool's payload is the range the model saw. Its text carries a
header naming the range, such as `[path · lines 1–2000 of 5312]`, and the
body below it. The header says `· capped` when the output cap ended the
read early, and names an empty range when the offset is past the end of
the file. A line is truncated at 2000 characters, counted in characters,
and a cut never splits a rune. A carriage return at the end of a line is
stripped, so a file with CRLF endings reads the same as one with LF
endings.

---

<!-- Source: reference/wire-api-mapping.md -->

# Wire API mapping

A paper round-trip through poo's internal message model, for the three wire
APIs the model has to survive: **Chat Completions**, **OpenAI Responses
(stateless)** and **Anthropic Messages**.

The question every row answers is the same one: if a provider sends a piece of
content, does poo's internal model hold it, and can poo put it back on the
wire unchanged?

The answer decides what the model has to carry. The model is frozen after this
document, so a gap found here is a gap fixed here.

## How to read the tables

- **Wire** is the JSON the API sees. Ellipses stand for the payload.
- **Internal** is poo's own shape, in the shorthand of the Go types
  (`Message{Role:user, Origin:user, Content:[text]}`).
- **Back** is what poo puts on the wire when it replays the same history.
- **Lossless** says whether `wire → internal → wire` keeps the meaning. It
  does not mean byte-for-byte: JSON whitespace and key order are not part of
  the meaning, but a value the API treats as opaque **is** part of it.

The internal model is:

```go
type Message struct {
    Role         Role
    Content      []ContentBlock
    ID           string          // "m<n>", session-monotonic
    Origin       Origin          // "user", "model", "job", "system", ...
    DeliveryNote *DeliveryNote   // what the user had seen of the last reply
}

type ContentBlock struct {
    Kind        ContentKind      // text | thinking | tool_call | tool_result | provider
    Text        string
    ToolCallID  string
    Name        string
    Arguments   json.RawMessage
    IsError     bool
    Provider    *ProviderBlock   // opaque provider data
}

type ProviderBlock struct {
    API      API               // chat_completions | responses | anthropic_messages
    Type     string            // the provider's own name for the payload
    Data     json.RawMessage   // the payload, verbatim
    Required bool              // the request fails without it
}
```

A `ProviderBlock` is the plan's first-class opaque block. It rides either
alone (a `provider` content block) or as the companion of a visible block (a
thinking block's signature).

## Chat Completions

`POST /v1/chat/completions`. The API poo v1 ships.

| # | Wire | Internal | Back | Lossless |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | `{"role":"system","content":"…"}` | `Message{Role:system, Origin:system, Content:[text]}` | the same message | **yes** |
| C2 | `{"role":"user","content":"…"}` | `Message{Role:user, Origin:user, Content:[text]}` | the same message | **yes** |
| C3 | `{"role":"assistant","content":"…"}` | `Message{Role:assistant, Origin:model, ID:"m3", Content:[text]}` | the same message, without the id | **yes** — the id is poo's, not the API's |
| C4 | `{"role":"assistant","content":null,"tool_calls":[{"id":"call_1","type":"function","function":{"name":"bash","arguments":"{\"command\":\"ls\"}"}}]}` | `Content{kind:tool_call, tool_call_id:"call_1", name:"bash", arguments:{"command":"ls"}}` | the same call, with the arguments re-encoded as a JSON string | **yes, in value** — the wire carries the arguments as a *string*; poo holds the parsed value, so whitespace inside that string is not preserved |
| C5 | `{"role":"tool","tool_call_id":"call_1","content":"out"}` | `Message{Role:tool, Origin:tool, Content:[{kind:tool_result, tool_call_id:"call_1", name:"bash", text:"out"}]}` | the same message | **yes**, except the two fields the wire has no room for: the tool's `name` (read back from the matching call) and `is_error` (conveyed in the text) |
| C6 | `delta.reasoning_content` (a server extension, not in the spec) | `Content{kind:thinking, text}` | dropped | **no** — Chat Completions has no field that carries thinking back. The model keeps the thinking in the view; the request loses it. |
| C7 | `delta.tool_calls[]` fragments | `Content{kind:tool_call}` | reassembled | **yes** |
| C8 | `usage.prompt_tokens`, `usage.completion_tokens`, `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` | `UsageReport{InputTokens, OutputTokens, CacheReadTokens}` | — (response side) | **yes** |
| C9 | `finish_reason: "stop"｜"length"｜"tool_calls"` | `FinishReason` | the same | **yes** |
| C10 | `tools[].function.{name,description,parameters}` | `ToolSpec{Name, Description, Schema}` | the same | **yes** |
| C11 | `{"role":"assistant","content":null,"refusal":"…"}` — a refusal is a **top-level string** on the message, not a content part | `Content{kind:text}` | a plain string | **no** — see *Scope decisions* |

Two asymmetries are worth naming because they are properties of the API, not
of poo's model:

- **Thinking does not survive the request.** `reasoning_content` is an
  extension many servers send and no server accepts back. A history that
  carries thinking is a history the endpoint never sees again.
- **A tool result carries no error flag.** Chat Completions has no
  `is_error` on a tool message: the failure is in the text the model reads.
  poo keeps `is_error` in its own record and in the model's view, because
  Anthropic has a field for it and the two APIs should not behave
  differently inside poo.

## OpenAI Responses (stateless)

`POST /v1/responses`, with no `previous_response_id` and no `store`: every
request carries the whole history, which is poo's rule.

| # | Wire | Internal | Back | Lossless |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | `{"type":"message","role":"user","content":[{"type":"input_text","text":"…"}]}` | `Message{Role:user, Origin:user, Content:[text]}` | a message item with `input_text` | **yes** |
| R2 | `{"type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"output_text","text":"…"}]}` | `Message{Role:assistant, Origin:model, Content:[text]}` | a message item with `output_text` | **yes** |
| R3 | `{"type":"function_call","call_id":"call_1","name":"bash","arguments":"{\"command\":\"ls\"}"}` | `Content{kind:tool_call, tool_call_id:"call_1", name:"bash", arguments:{"command":"ls"}}` | its own item, arguments re-encoded as a string | **yes, in value** |
| R4 | `{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":"call_1","output":"…"}` | `Content{kind:tool_result, tool_call_id:"call_1", text:"…"}` | its own item | **yes** |
| R5 | `{"type":"reasoning","id":"rs_1","summary":[{"type":"summary_text","text":"…"}],"encrypted_content":"…"}` | `Content{kind:thinking, text:"…", provider:{api:responses, type:"reasoning", data:{"id":"rs_1","encrypted_content":"…"}}}` | one reasoning item again: the summary from the thinking text, the id and the encrypted content from the provider block | **in the summary shape** — the encrypted content is opaque and travels back untouched, and the summary's text survives. The *part* boundaries do not: the thinking is one string, so a summary of several parts comes back as one part. See *Where this document is not sure*. |
| R6 | a compaction item (an opaque item the provider's own compaction produced) | `Content{kind:provider, provider:{api:responses, type:"compaction", data:<the item, verbatim>, required:true}}` | the same item, verbatim | **yes** — the payload is never interpreted, only carried |
| R7 | `instructions` (the system prompt) | `Message{Role:system, Origin:system, Content:[text]}` | the `instructions` field | **yes, in content** — the field's shape differs, the prompt does not |
| R8 | `usage.input_tokens`, `usage.output_tokens`, `usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens` | `UsageReport` | — (response side) | **yes** |
| R9 | `max_output_tokens` | `ChatRequest.MaxTokens` | the same | **yes** |
| R10 | `{"type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"refusal","refusal":"…"}]}` — a refusal is a **content part** here, unlike Chat Completions | `Content{kind:text}` | a plain string | **no** — see *Scope decisions* |

The structural difference from Chat Completions is that a function call and
its output are **top-level items**, not messages. poo's model keeps a tool
call as a block of the assistant message, so the transport splits one
assistant message into a message item plus one item per call, in order. The
order is preserved, because the API matches a call to its output by position
as well as by id.

## Anthropic Messages

`POST /v1/messages`.

| # | Wire | Internal | Back | Lossless |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | `system` (a string or a list of blocks) | `Message{Role:system, Origin:system, Content:[text]}` | the `system` field | **yes, in content** |
| A2 | `{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"…"}]}` | `Message{Role:user, Origin:user, Content:[text]}` | the same | **yes** |
| A3 | `{"role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"…"}]}` | `Message{Role:assistant, Origin:model, Content:[text]}` | the same | **yes** |
| A4 | `{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_1","name":"bash","input":{"command":"ls"}}` | `Content{kind:tool_call, tool_call_id:"toolu_1", name:"bash", arguments:{"command":"ls"}}` | the same block | **yes** — the input is a JSON *object* here, not a string |
| A5 | `{"type":"tool_result","tool_use_id":"toolu_1","content":"…","is_error":false}` | `Content{kind:tool_result, tool_call_id:"toolu_1", text:"…", is_error:false}` | the same block | **yes** — the tool's name is not on the wire, and poo does not need it there |
| A6 | `{"type":"thinking","thinking":"…","signature":"sig"}` | `Content{kind:thinking, text:"…", provider:{api:anthropic_messages, type:"thinking_signature", data:"\"sig\""}}` | one thinking block again: the text from the block, the signature from the provider block | **yes** — the signature is opaque and must travel back untouched |
| A7 | `{"type":"redacted_thinking","data":"…"}` | `Content{kind:provider, provider:{api:anthropic_messages, type:"redacted_thinking", data:"\"…\""}}` | the same block, verbatim | **yes** |
| A8 | `stop_reason: "end_turn"｜"max_tokens"｜"tool_use"` | `FinishReason` | the same, mapped | **yes** |
| A9 | `usage.input_tokens`, `usage.output_tokens`, `usage.cache_read_input_tokens`, `usage.cache_creation_input_tokens` | `UsageReport{InputTokens, OutputTokens, CacheReadTokens}` | — (response side) | **yes**, except the cache *write* count, which the plan's usage record has no field for. See *Scope decisions*. |

Two placement rules belong to the API, and a transport has to honour them:

- A tool result lives in a **user** message, not in one of its own. poo keeps
  tool results in their own message with `role: tool`; the transport merges
  them into the user message that follows the assistant's `tool_use`.
- Thinking blocks come **first** in an assistant message. poo preserves block
  order, so the transport keeps the order and the rule holds.

## Gaps this round trip found, and how they are closed

1. **Opaque provider data had nowhere to go.** Anthropic's thinking
   signature, Anthropic's redacted thinking, the Responses reasoning item's
   encrypted content and the Responses compaction item are all values the
   model must hold without interpreting them, and must give back unchanged.
   *Closed:* `ProviderBlock{api, type, data, required}` is a first-class
   block. It rides alone as a `provider` content block, or as the companion
   of a visible block (a thinking block's signature).

2. **A visible block needed room for an invisible companion.** The
   Anthropic thinking block is one block on the wire and two facts in poo:
   the thinking text and the signature. Splitting it into two blocks would
   break the "one thinking block" shape the API expects.
   *Closed:* a content block carries an optional `Provider` companion. The
   transport merges the two back into the API's own block.

3. **Messages had no id.** The plan's delivery note names an assistant
   message, and the message id is what the note refers to.
   *Closed:* `Message.ID` holds a session-monotonic `m<n>`, and
   `poo.MessageIDs` hands them out. The counter belongs to the session, so
   a second run's ids continue where the first run's stopped.

4. **Messages had no origin.** A user message can come from a person, a
   steer, an interrupt, a follow-up, a job or a hook, and the model and the
   log both need to know which.
   *Closed:* `Message.Origin`, with the plan's values.

5. **A user message had nowhere to put a delivery note.** The note is
   rendered when the input is delivered, prefixed to the message's text,
   and must survive to the record, so replay is exact.
   *Closed:* `Message.DeliveryNote{message_id, upto_chars, text}`.

6. **A tool result's tool name and error flag have no home on one of the
   APIs.** Chat Completions' tool message carries neither.
   *Closed:* this is not a model gap. poo holds both, the transport sends
   what the API accepts, and the difference is recorded in the mapping above
   rather than worked around in the model.

## Scope decisions

These are deliberate, and they are not gaps in the model:

- **Refusal parts** are not represented. The two APIs differ in where a
  refusal lives: the Responses API sends it as a `refusal` content part
  (`{"type":"refusal","refusal":"…"}`), and Chat Completions sends it as
  a top-level `message.refusal` string next to the content. v1 ships one
  transport, the plan's block list does not name refusal, and a refusal is
  only distinguishable by the message's shape — a shape the
  OpenAI-compatible servers v1 targets do not all accept. The refusal text
  is kept as a text block, so nothing the model said is lost; what is
  lost is the *label*.
- **An attachment a tool returns** — an image or a recording — is carried as
  its own block, and its place on the wire belongs to the API. Chat Completions
  takes one only in a user message, so this transport sends the tool message
  and then a user message carrying the parts: `image_url` for an image, and
  `input_audio` with the base64 and a `wav` or `mp3` format for audio. No
  Responses or Messages transport ships here; when one does, its own field
  takes the block without the extra message, since the Responses API names
  `input_image` and `input_audio` inside the tool result's output. The Messages
  API has no audio block, so a Messages transport carries images and refuses
  audio.
- **The cache-write token count** (Anthropic's
  `cache_creation_input_tokens`) has no field: the plan's usage record names
  `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_read_tokens` and `ttft_ms`, and
  this stage adds no field to that vocabulary.
- **A foreign API's opaque block** is omitted from a request when it is not
  required, and fails the request with `session_incompatible` when it is.
  The rule needs no model change: the block says which API it belongs to.

## Where this document is not sure

Stated plainly, because a wrong detail in a mapping is a bug that waits for
the transport that implements it:

- **The Responses compaction item.** The API has a compaction endpoint that
  returns a compacted item set including a compaction item with encrypted
  content. The exact field names of that item are not pinned here. The model
  does not care: the item is carried verbatim in a `provider` block, and the
  transport that implements the endpoint is the only thing that has to know
  its shape.
- **The Responses reasoning item's `summary` versus `content`.** A
  reasoning item carries either a `summary` (a list of `summary_text`
  parts) or `content` (a list of `reasoning_text` parts), and the two
  hold different things: the summary is the model's own account of its
  reasoning, and the content is the reasoning itself. poo's model has one
  thinking string, so the *text* survives in either shape but the *part
  boundaries* do not, and an item whose reasoning arrived as `content`
  cannot be told from one whose summary said the same words. The
  transport that implements the Responses API must decide how the two
  shapes map onto the one block; the model does not depend on the answer,
  because the opaque `encrypted_content` is carried verbatim either way.
- **Whether the Responses API accepts a `system`-role message item.** The
  documented way to send a system prompt is the top-level `instructions`
  field, and that is what the mapping uses. A system-role item is not
  assumed to work.
- **Anthropic's exact ordering rule for thinking blocks.** The rule used
  here is that thinking blocks come first in an assistant message. The
  transport that implements Anthropic must confirm it against the API
  before it ships; the model does not depend on the answer, because it keeps
  the blocks in order either way.
- **The Chat Completions content-part array.** The `text` and `refusal` part
  types are part of the newer spec; the servers poo targets mostly take a
  plain string. poo sends a string. A refusal, when the server sends one
  at all, arrives as the message's top-level `refusal` string, not as a
  part.
- **Anthropic's `cache_creation_input_tokens`.** The field name is taken
  from the usage block's shape; the value is not carried, so a wrong guess
  costs nothing.

## What the model therefore has to carry

The three APIs together need: text, thinking, tool calls, tool results, one
opaque companion per visible block, and whole opaque items. That is exactly
`ContentKind`'s five values plus `ProviderBlock`, and nothing more. The model
is frozen.

---

<!-- Source: reference/evals.md -->

# Evals & Benchmarks

`poo` uses two evaluation tracks:

1. **Built-in `poo-eval` suite** — 20 local tasks for regression testing, baseline comparisons, and failure-mode analysis.
2. **Harbor adapter (`evals/harbor/`)** — external benchmark runs on Terminal-Bench and SWE-bench, including head-to-head comparisons against other CLI harnesses.

## Built-in `poo-eval` suite

The suite contains 20 tasks across three categories:

- **12 coding tasks**: Python packages with a bug and a failing `unittest` suite. Before grading, the harness restores the fixture's original test files so a run cannot pass by rewriting tests; test edits are reported as unexpected changes.
- **5 find-and-explain tasks**: Read-only repositories with one question and no files to change. `evals/tasks/check_answer.py` derives the required facts directly from the untouched workdir, asserts zero file edits, and verifies that the final message names every requested fact.
- **3 long-context tasks**: Working sets sized past a 32,768-token window and well under 262,144 tokens (`long-find-definition-in-tree`, `long-find-error-in-log`, `long-change-timeout-everywhere`). They test search discipline, narrowing large files, and multi-file edits without blind search-and-replace. (`long-change-timeout-everywhere` is the only task whose prompt expects test updates.)

Each task lives in `evals/tasks/<id>/` with a `task.json` and `check.sh` (exit `0` = solved). The model catalog is `evals/models.yaml`, and task repositories live under `evals/fixtures/`.

### Running and managing baselines

Run the suite against one or more models from `evals/models.yaml`:

```bash
poo-eval run --models gemma4,qwen --seeds 3
```

Each run writes its report and raw transcripts (`runs/`) to an ignored directory at `evals/runs/<date>-<git sha>/`. Nothing is committed until accepted:

```bash
# Promote a run's report.json, report.md, and summary.json to evals/baseline/
poo-eval accept evals/runs/<date>-<git sha>

# Compare a candidate run against the accepted baseline
poo-eval compare evals/runs/<date>-<git sha>

# Or compare two explicit run directories
poo-eval compare <baseline-dir> <candidate-dir>
```

`compare` writes its diff into the candidate directory. Commit updated `evals/baseline/` files in the same PR that produced the run; older baselines remain in git history.

### Isolation (`--isolation bwrap`)

`poo-eval run` wraps each `poo` process in `bubblewrap` by default (`--isolation bwrap`). Inside the sandbox, the process sees only:

- Read-only `/usr` and `/etc`
- Its own workdir at `/work`
- Its log directory at `/log`
- A private `/tmp` that also serves as `$HOME` (keeping user-level installs like `pip install --user` out of the run's diff)
- Its own PID namespace (closing `/proc` access to host processes)
- Shared network access so model endpoints remain reachable

The real home directory, repository, and task set are hidden. `check.sh` runs outside the sandbox so it can access the task set, which means pass/fail status is determined outside the model's reach. Workdirs are created under `<user cache dir>/poo-eval/work` (`--work-root` overrides this and rejects any path containing or inside the task set).

Passing `--isolation none` disables `bwrap` and runs model commands with your full privileges. Without sandboxing, a model that searches the filesystem can discover `check.sh` or `check_answer.py`, invalidating the result.

### Fixture integrity hashing

Before the first run, each invocation snapshots the fixtures its tasks use into `<work root>/<invocation>/fixtures/` and builds every workdir from that snapshot. The runner hashes each source fixture, its snapshot, and each task directory at startup and again after every run.

If any hash changes, the run is marked invalid (`source_changed`, `success: false`), a warning naming the run is written to `stderr`, and `poo-eval run` exits non-zero without restoring the modified source.

---

## Harbor adapter (`evals/harbor/`)

The Harbor adapter (`evals/harbor/`, added in PR #344) integrates `poo` with [Harbor](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor) via `poo_agent:PooAgent`. It uploads a static Linux `poo` binary into each task container, runs `poo run` headlessly, and reports token usage and session metrics back to Harbor.

### Prerequisites and building the static binary

1. Install Harbor (`uv tool install harbor`) and ensure a container runtime is available (Docker, rootless Podman with `podman.socket` and `DOCKER_HOST`, or a remote backend such as `--env modal` or `--env daytona`).
2. Build the static Linux binary (`CGO_ENABLED=0`) so it runs in any Linux task image with no libc dependencies:

```bash
evals/harbor/build-bin.sh
```

This writes `evals/harbor/bin/poo-linux-<arch>`. Re-run it after any change to `poo`.

### Running Terminal-Bench and SWE-bench

Run a quick smoke test on Terminal-Bench before running the full suite:

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."

PYTHONPATH=evals/harbor harbor run \
  --dataset terminal-bench/terminal-bench@4.1.0 \
  --agent poo_agent:PooAgent \
  --model openai/gpt-4o \
  --ak context_limit=128000 \
  --ak max_turns=80 \
  --n-tasks 3 \
  --n-concurrent 2
```

The same adapter runs against SWE-bench Verified (`--dataset swebench-verified`) or any other Harbor dataset. For local or homelab OpenAI-compatible endpoints, pass `--ak endpoint=...` and `--ak model_id=...` using a LAN hostname or container host alias (`host.containers.internal` / `host.docker.internal`) rather than `localhost`:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=evals/harbor harbor run \
  --dataset terminal-bench/terminal-bench@4.1.0 \
  --agent poo_agent:PooAgent \
  --ak endpoint=http://grace:4000/v1 \
  --ak model_id=qwen \
  --ak context_limit=131072 \
  --ak tools_mode=native \
  --n-tasks 3 \
  --n-concurrent 2
```

To pin compaction, sampling, or built-in providers, pass `--ak settings=/path/to/settings.yaml`. A settings run uses the model named in the file; overriding the model or window requires setting both `endpoint` and `model_id`.

### Paired harness comparisons

Harbor includes built-in adapters for other CLI harnesses, allowing head-to-head comparisons on the same dataset and model:

```bash
# Run poo
PYTHONPATH=evals/harbor harbor run \
  --dataset terminal-bench/terminal-bench@4.1.0 \
  --agent poo_agent:PooAgent \
  --model openai/gpt-4o \
  --ak context_limit=128000 \
  --n-tasks 15 \
  --n-concurrent 4

# Run another harness (e.g., opencode, claude-code, codex) on the same slice
harbor run \
  --dataset terminal-bench/terminal-bench@4.1.0 \
  --agent opencode \
  --model openai/gpt-4o \
  --n-tasks 15 \
  --n-concurrent 4
```

Results and raw `session.jsonl` transcripts are written under Harbor's `jobs/` directory.

### Key `--ak` options

| Key | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `poo_bin` | `evals/harbor/bin/poo-linux-<arch>` | Path to static Linux `poo` binary (or `POO_HARBOR_BIN`) |
| `settings` | none | Local `poo` settings file uploaded into `/logs/agent/` |
| `endpoint` | inferred from `--model` | OpenAI-compatible base URL (or `POO_ENDPOINT`) |
| `model_id` | inferred from `--model` | Model ID (`--model-id`) |
| `api_key_env` | inferred from `--model` | Host env var forwarded into container (or `POO_API_KEY_ENV`) |
| `context_limit` | `131072` | Context window in tokens (`--context-limit`) |
| `tools_mode` | none | `native`, `text`, or `auto` (`--tools-mode`) |
| `reasoning_effort` | none | Passed to `--reasoning-effort` |
| `max_turns` | none | Turn cap (`--max-turns`); unset leaves the run uncapped |
| `max_output` | none | Output token cap (`--max-output`) |
| `truncation_retries` | none | Retries after an output-limit cut (`--truncation-retries`) |
| `profile` | `code` | `poo` profile (`--profile`) |
| `context_strategy` | none | Compaction strategy (`--context-strategy`) |
| `context_keep_recent` | none | Compaction verbatim tail in tokens (`--context-keep-recent`) |
| `timeout` | none | Wall-clock limit, e.g. `15m` (`--timeout`) |
| `append_system_prompt` | none | Extra system prompt text (`--append-system-prompt`) |

Run the adapter's unit tests with:

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s evals/harbor -v
```

### Benchmark note

In head-to-head Terminal-Bench runs on locally hosted `glm-5.3-flash`, `poo` beat `pi` and tied `mini-swe-agent`. This is not an exhaustive multi-model benchmark study, but it provides concrete evidence that `poo` drives relentless agent loops effectively on real terminal tasks.
